1.pericope_label: For I would that ye knew what great conflict I have for you, and for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin describe the conflict and question the city. Gill says the words are occasioned by the previous chapter, where Paul laboured and strove according to the energy of divine power in him to present every man perfect in Christ; lest the Colossians should think those labours and strivings were only for the persons among whom he was and to whom he personally preached, he would have them know and assure themselves that the great conflict, strife and agony in which he was engaged was for them also. By this, Gill says, he means his fervent prayers and wrestlings with God, the conflicts he had in his own mind and with his own spirit about the good of the churches of Christ, the care of which was upon him, even of those to whom he was by face unknown, sometimes hoping, sometimes fearing, sometimes rejoicing, at other times weeping at what he heard concerning them; also his combats with the false apostles, striving and earnestly contending for the faith of the Gospel, giving no place to them, no, not for an hour, defending truth and refuting error. Calvin says Paul declares his affection towards them that he may have more credit and authority, for we readily believe those whom we know to be desirous of our welfare; and it is an evidence of no ordinary affection that he was concerned about them in the midst of death, that is, when he was in danger of his life. To express the intensity of his affection the more emphatically he calls it a contest, and Calvin does not find fault with the rendering of Erasmus, though the force of the Greek word is to be noticed. As there is commonly no love between those unknown to each other, Paul speaks slightingly of the acquaintance contracted from sight, for among the servants of God there is a sight different from that of the flesh which excites love. Calvin adds that since it is almost universally agreed that the First Epistle to Timothy was written from Laodicea, some on that account assign to Galatia the Laodicea mentioned here, the other being the metropolis of Phrygia Pacatiana; but it seems to him more probable that that inscription is incorrect.

Henry observes the great concern Paul had for the Colossians and the other churches of which he had no personal knowledge. The apostle had never been at Colosse, and the church planted there was not of his planting, yet he had as tender a care of it as if it had been the only people of his charge. Paul's care of the church, Henry says, was such as amounted to a conflict: he was in a sort of agony, and had a constant fear respecting what would become of them, and herein he was a follower of his Master, who was in an agony for us and was heard in that he feared. Henry draws the lesson that we may keep up a communion by faith, hope and holy love even with those churches and fellow-Christians of whom we have no personal knowledge and with whom we have no conversation; we can think, and pray, and be concerned for one another at the greatest distance, and those we never saw in the flesh we may hope to meet in heaven.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the word and the geography. Barnes says the Greek word is agona, not the word rendered agony in Luke 22:44, though that is derived from it; the same word is rendered conflict in Philippians 1:30, contention in 1 Thessalonians 2:2, fight in 1 Timothy 6:12 and 2 Timothy 4:7, and race in Hebrews 12:1. It properly refers to the combats, contests, struggles and efforts at the public games, the toil and conflict to obtain a victory, and refers here to the anxious care, the mental conflict, the earnest solicitude which Paul had on their behalf in view of the dangers to which they were exposed from Judaizing Christians and pagan philosophy. The margin gives fear, or care. Laodicea, he says, was the capital of Phrygia in Asia Minor, a little south of Colosse, and there was a church early planted there, the lukewarm church mentioned in Revelation 3:14; being in the vicinity of Colosse it was exposed to the same perils, and the rebuke there showed that the fears of Paul were well founded and that the arts of the false teachers were too successful. Ellicott notes that the word is repeated from the striving of the previous verse, being in the original the cognate verb, and that it describes the intense earnestness of the whole struggle against evil which Paul was undergoing for them; but looking at Colossians 4:12 he would refer it especially to striving in prayer, and thinks it is dwelt upon here to show why, although unknown to them personally, he yet writes so urgently. The three cities lay near together in the valley of the Lycus, a tributary of the Maeander; probably they were converted at one time and are evidently regarded as forming one Christian community, for which Epaphras, the evangelist of Colossae, felt himself responsible. Laodicea was the greatest and richest of the three, and we have no further notice of it in Scripture except the stern apocalyptic letter which has made its name proverbial for spiritual luke-warmness and presumptuous self-reliance. Hierapolis and Laodicea play a prominent part in the subsequent history of Christianity in Asia Minor, while Colossae never attains importance and has left but few and meagre remains. The description of those who have not seen his face doubtless indicates Hierapolis, but the context shows that it also includes Colossae; and if the reading taken at Colossians 1:7 is correct, Epaphras had been commissioned by Paul, so that indirectly the Apostle might be held to be the founder of Colossae, this letter standing midway between the unreserved familiarity of the Epistles to Corinth or Philippi and the more formal reserve of the Epistle to the Romans. Robertson renders it literally, how great a contest I am having, notes that the old adjectival relative used for age or size occurs in the New Testament only here and twice in James 3:5, and calls it an inward contest of anxiety like the care for all the churches of 2 Corinthians 11:28, carrying on the metaphor of the striving of Colossians 1:29. Paul's concern extended beyond Colossae to Laodicea and to Hierapolis, the three great cities in the Lycus Valley where Gnosticism was beginning to do harm. The phrase about those who have not seen his face undoubtedly includes Hierapolis, and a few late manuscripts actually insert it here; the language includes all in that whole region who have not seen Paul's face in person, and the perfect active form used has two peculiarities of spelling.

Clarke and Wesley give the sense of the word and the standing of the readers. Clarke says the word which we render conflict is to be understood as implying earnest care and solicitude, accompanied undoubtedly with the most fervent application to the throne of grace on their behalf, and that the participle of the preceding verse gave the apostle occasion to use it here: he agonized with God, and his agony was for them. Laodicea, Clarke says, was a city of Asia Minor on the borders of Caria, Phrygia and Lydia, originally called Diospolis, or the city of Jupiter, and afterwards Rhoas, but obtaining the name of Laodicea from Laodice the wife of Antiochus, and now called Ladik; it was formerly celebrated for its commerce and for the fine black wool of its sheep, and Colosse lay between it and Hierapolis, itself a town of Phrygia famous for its hot baths. From the words about those who have not seen his face it has been conjectured that Paul had never been at either Colosse or Laodicea, and from the letter of the text this appears probable; yet his having passed more than once through this country, preaching and strengthening the churches, renders it very improbable, and it is therefore most likely that the apostle speaks collectively, having the most earnest concern not only for the churches with which he was acquainted but also for those to whom he was not personally known. Wesley glosses the conflict as one of care, desire and prayer, and notes that because so many had not seen his face, Paul in writing to the Colossians refrains from those familiar appellations, Brethren and Beloved.

debates: What the conflict was. Barnes takes the word from the public games and applies it to anxious care and mental conflict; Ellicott, from the cognate verb of the previous verse and a later verse of the letter, refers it especially to striving in prayer; Clarke joins earnest solicitude to fervent application at the throne of grace; Gill divides it between wrestling with God for the churches and combat with the false apostles; Henry calls it an agony and a constant fear.

Whether Paul had been to Colosse. Clarke grants that the letter of the text makes it probable he had not, but calls this very improbable since he had passed more than once through the country, and takes the apostle to be speaking collectively; Ellicott holds that the clause includes Colosse and that Paul might indirectly be the founder there through Epaphras, reading the tone of the letter as midway between familiarity and reserve; Henry takes it plainly that Paul had never been there.

Which Laodicea is meant. Calvin reports that some, on the ground that the First Epistle to Timothy was written from Laodicea, assign the Laodicea named here to Galatia; he judges that inscription incorrect. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all take it for the city of the Lycus valley without question.
outliers: Calvin alone treats the verse as a piece of rhetorical strategy, holding that Paul discloses his affection in order to gain credit and authority with readers who had never met him.
Wesley alone reasons from the verse to the style of the letter, inferring that because so many of the readers had not seen Paul's face he withholds the familiar appellations Brethren and Beloved.

2.pericope_label: That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ; in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the comfort, the assurance and the treasures. Gill says the consolation of their hearts is one reason why the apostle had so great a conflict, and why he desired them to know it. The hearts of God's people often need comfort by reason of indwelling sin, the temptations of Satan, the hidings of God's face and afflictive providences, and also by reason of false teachers, who greatly trouble them, unsettle their minds, weaken their faith and fill them with doubts and perplexities, which was the case with these churches. The business of Gospel ministers is to comfort such; the doctrines of the Gospel are calculated for this very purpose, such as full redemption, free justification, complete pardon of sin, peace and reconciliation. On the treasures Gill allows two readings: either the mystery of the Gospel, which contains the rich mines and hidden treasures of all divine truths, so called because of their intrinsic value and because of their variety and abundance, being the unsearchable riches of Christ; or Christ himself, and not so much his personal wisdom as God or as man or as Mediator, but that fulness of truth as well as grace which dwells in him as in its subject and fountain, by whom it comes and from whom it is derived to us, our highest wisdom lying in knowing him. Calvin says Paul now intimates what he desires for them and shews that his affection is truly apostolic, since he desires nothing else than that they may be united together in faith and love: when mutually agreed in one faith we are also joined together in mutual love, and this is the solid joy of a pious mind and the blessed life. The bond of holy unity is the truth of God when we embrace it with one consent. Since many, contenting themselves with a slight taste, have nothing but a confused and evanescent knowledge, Paul mentions the full assurance expressly, meaning by it full and clear perception, and admonishing them that according to the measure of understanding they must make progress also in love. In that term he distinguishes between faith and mere opinion, for a man truly knows the Lord who does not vacillate or waver in doubt but stands fast in a firm and constant persuasion; this constancy and stability Paul always connects with faith, as it can no more be separated from it than heat or light from the sun, and the doctrine of the schoolmen is therefore devilish, inasmuch as it takes away assurance. The knowledge in question is nothing else than the knowledge of the gospel, and the gospel can be understood by faith alone, not by reason or the perspicacity of the human understanding. Calvin takes the mystery of God passively, as that in which God is revealed, and says God cannot be known otherwise than in Christ, so that all who think they know anything of God apart from Christ contrive to themselves an idol in the place of God; the passage is memorable for proving Christ's divinity and the unity of his essence with the Father. On the treasures Calvin says all the wisdom and knowledge of the pious are hid in Christ, so that we are perfect in wisdom if we truly know him and it is madness to wish to know anything besides him; they are called hidden because they are not seen glittering with great splendour but lie hid, as it were, under the contemptible abasement and simplicity of the cross, since the preaching of the cross is always foolishness to the perishing. He reckons no great difference between wisdom and knowledge here, the two terms serving only to give additional strength, as though Paul had said that no knowledge, erudition, learning or wisdom can be found elsewhere.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the words and the text. Barnes says the same verb occurs at Ephesians 4:16 rendered compacted, at Acts 9:22 proving, at Acts 16:10 assuredly gathering, at 1 Corinthians 2:16 instruct, and here and at Colossians 2:19 knit together; it means properly to make to come together, and hence refers to a firm union where the hearts of Christians are one. The way of comforting each other was by solid Christian friendship, and the means of cementing that was love: not a mere outward profession or a merely speculative faith, but a union of affection. The full understanding of the mystery was an invaluable possession, like abundant wealth, and if they were divided in affection and split into factions they could not hope to secure it. The word rendered full assurance means firm persuasion, settled conviction, and is rendered assurance or full assurance in every instance where it occurs. The mystery means the doctrine respecting God which had before been concealed but was now revealed in the gospel; it does not mean that anything about the doctrine was unintelligible once made known. The hitherto unrevealed truth related to the fact that God subsisted in more persons than one, as Father and as Christ. Barnes reports great variety of reading in the manuscripts on the whole clause, and that many critics regard it as spurious, but he does not see evidence that it is not genuine, and the strain of the apostle's exhortation seems to him to demand it. On the treasures, he says the correct translation is in whom, the reference being doubtless to Christ, whose name is the immediate antecedent; are hid means like treasures concealed or garnered up, not that none of them had been developed, but that Christ as Mediator was the great treasure-house where all the wisdom and knowledge needful for men were to be found, so that it is not necessary to apply to philosophy or to the teachings of men. Ellicott glosses comforted as encouraged or strengthened, both to stand fast and to advance in the faith. The verb has two senses, to knit together, as at Colossians 2:19 and Ephesians 4:16, and to carry with us in argument, that is to instruct or convince, as at Acts 9:22, Acts 16:10 and 1 Corinthians 2:16; either would give good sense, but the usage in this and the Ephesian Epistle and the addition of the words in love are decisive for the former. The idea of the passage is precisely that of Philippians 1:9, that their love may abound more and more in knowledge and in all judgment: Paul bids them seek the fulness of intelligence not through the rashness of speculation but through the insight of love, for Christian knowledge is the knowledge of a personal Saviour, and in all personal knowledge he knows best who loves best. The clause about the acknowledgement is altogether obscured in our version and should be rendered, to the full knowledge of the mystery of God, which is Christ: at Colossians 1:27 Christ indwelling is the mystery that solves the problem of humanity, while here Christ is He in whom the inscrutable nature of God is revealed. On the treasures Ellicott notes that the order of the original is curious, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, as hidden treasures; the word hidden is an almost technical word for secret teaching given only to the initiated, used originally as a term of honour and afterwards, from the character of the books so called, coming to signify spurious and heretical. Paul evidently takes up a word used by the pretenders to a special and abstruse knowledge and applies it to the heavenly things which He alone knows who is in heaven. Knowledge, Ellicott adds, was the watchword of Gnosticism, the unbridled and fantastic spirit of metaphysical and religious speculation then beginning to infest all Christian thought, and it can hardly be accidental that Paul here subordinates it to the higher gift of wisdom. Robertson parses the verb as causal of the verb to go, to make go together, to coalesce in argument, in spiritual growth, and in love as here, and calls love the bond that binds all together. He notes a probable distinction between in, love as the sphere, and unto, as the goal, and says Paul desires the full use of the intellect in grasping the great mystery of Christ, which calls for the full and balanced exercise of all one's mental powers; the word for full and additional knowledge is Paul's reply to the Gnostics with their limited and perverted knowledge. The manuscripts differ widely on the last clause, but Robertson reads the mystery of God, even Christ: Christ is the mystery of God, no longer hidden but manifested, and meant for us to know to the fulness of our capacity. On the treasures he notes the old word behind our thesaurus, for coffer, storehouse, treasure, and says Paul confronts these pretentious intellectuals with the bold claim that Christ sums up all wisdom and knowledge; the treasures are hidden away whether the Gnostics have discovered them or not, and they are there in Christ as every believer knows by fresh and repeated discovery.

Clarke and Wesley give the image and the sense. Clarke says the verse means that they might have continual happiness in God, having constant affiance in him, and that the participle rendered knit together signifies being united as the beams or the timbers of a building are, by mortices and pins; the visible Church of Christ cannot be in union with God unless it have unity in itself, and without love this unity is impossible. The riches of the full assurance of understanding mean that they might have the most indubitable certainty of the truth of Christianity, of their own salvation and of the general design of God to admit the Gentiles into his Church, which is the grand mystery now laid open by the preaching of the Gospel. On the words that follow, Clarke lists the many forms found in different manuscripts, versions and fathers: the mystery of God, of God in Christ, of God who is in Christ, of God concerning Christ, of God who is Christ, of the God Christ, of God and Christ, of God the Father of Christ, of God the Father in Christ, and others; this great variety leaves the strongest presumption that the words in question are glosses which have crept into the text and are of no authority, and Griesbach has left them out of the text. On the treasures Clarke refers the phrase not to Christ but to the mystery mentioned above: in this glorious scheme of Christianity all the abundance and excellency of wisdom and knowledge are contained, and no scheme of salvation or divine knowledge ever equalled the Gospel plan in depth and excellency, a scheme which the wisdom of God alone could devise and which his power and infinite mercy alone could accomplish. Wesley glosses the whole clause briefly as the fullest and clearest understanding and knowledge of the gospel.

debates: What knit together means. Barnes takes it as a firm union of affection, love being the cement; Ellicott allows the sense to convince but rules it out here on the usage of this letter and of Ephesians and on the added words in love; Robertson agrees and calls love the binding bond; Clarke gives the builder's image of beams joined by mortices and pins.

Whether the words about the Father and Christ are genuine. Clarke holds that the sheer variety of readings in the manuscripts, versions and fathers proves them glosses of no authority, and notes that Griesbach dropped them; Barnes reports the same variety and that many critics call the clause spurious, but sees no evidence against it and thinks the strain of the exhortation demands it; Ellicott and Robertson read a shorter text making Christ himself the mystery of God.

What the treasures are hid in. Clarke refers the phrase to the mystery, that is to the scheme of Christianity; Barnes says the correct translation is in whom, the reference being to Christ as the immediate antecedent; Robertson says it makes no real difference since Christ is the mystery of God; Gill allows either.

Why the treasures are called hidden. Ellicott takes the word as one borrowed from the pretenders to secret initiated teaching and turned against them; Robertson says they are hidden whether the Gnostics have found them or not; Calvin says they are hidden because they lie under the abasement and simplicity of the cross rather than glittering with splendour.
outliers: Calvin alone turns the phrase into a polemic against the schools, holding that because full assurance is inseparable from faith, a doctrine which substitutes conjecture for assurance is devilish.

Ellicott alone reverses the expected order of love and knowledge, making love the road to intelligence rather than its fruit, on the ground that in all personal knowledge he knows best who loves best.

4.pericope_label: And this I say, lest any man should beguile you with enticing words. For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin give the reference of the words and the ground of the confidence. Gill says the apostle means all that he had just said: that he had such a conflict for them, had told them of his care and fear on their account, had signified his great desire that they might arrive at a larger and more certain knowledge of the mysteries of grace, and had asserted that all solid spiritual wisdom and knowledge were in Christ. All this he said to show his affection for them, to observe to them that there was no need to seek for wisdom and knowledge elsewhere, since there was such a fulness of it in Christ and in the Gospel, and to put them upon their guard against false teachers. On the next verse Gill says the apostle anticipates an objection, how he could have such a conflict and concern for them and know so much of their affairs when he was absent from them and had never been among them; that he had never been corporeally present with them he owns, but this did not hinder that he might be present in another sense, and so have cognizance of them and their state. Calvin says that as the contrivances of men have an appearance of wisdom, the minds of the pious ought to be preoccupied with the persuasion that the knowledge of Christ is of itself amply sufficient, and that this is the key which can close the door against all base errors. The reason why mankind have involved themselves in so many wicked opinions, so many idolatries and so many foolish speculations, is that, despising the simplicity of the gospel, they have ventured to aspire higher; all the errors in Popery must be reckoned as proceeding from this ingratitude, that, not resting satisfied with Christ alone, men have given themselves up to strange doctrines. Calvin compares the way the writer to the Hebrews exhorts believers not to be led astray by strange or new doctrines by first laying the foundation that Christ is the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever: those are out of danger who remain in Christ, while those not satisfied with Christ are exposed to all fallacies. It is not lawful, Paul would have every one hold, for a Christian man to know anything except Christ; everything brought forward after this, have it ever so imposing an appearance, will be of no value, and no persuasiveness of speech can turn aside so much as the breadth of a finger the minds of those that have devoted their understanding to Christ. On the next verse Calvin says that lest any should object that the admonition was unseasonable as coming from a place so remote, Paul says his affection towards them made him present and able to judge what is expedient for them as though he were there; and by praising their present condition he admonishes them not to fall back from it or turn aside, saying in effect, go on as you have begun. By order he means agreement, no less than duly regulated morals and entire discipline, and he commends their faith in respect of its constancy and steadfastness, meaning that it is an empty shadow of faith when the mind wavers and vacillates between different opinions.

Henry treats the verse as a caution against deceivers, joining it with the warning of the eighth verse against being spoiled. The apostle insists so much on the perfection of Christ and of the gospel revelation in order to preserve them from the ensnaring insinuations of those who would corrupt their principles. The way in which Satan spoils souls, Henry says, is by beguiling them: he deceives them, and by this means slays them; he is the old serpent who beguiled Eve through his subtlety, and he could not ruin us if he did not cheat us, and could not cheat us but by our own fault and folly. Satan's agents, who aim to spoil them, beguile them with enticing words; and Henry bids the reader see the danger of enticing words, and how many are ruined by the flattery of those who lie in wait to deceive and by the false disguises and fair appearances of evil principles and wicked practices. They ought to stand upon their guard against enticing words and be aware and afraid of those who would entice them to any evil, for what such men aim at is to spoil them.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson define the words and the danger. Barnes says the phrase refers to the character and sufficiency of the truth revealed in Christ, that to beguile is to deceive and lead away from the truth, and that enticing words are artful words, smooth and plausible arguments such as were employed by the Greek sophists and rhetoricians. On the next verse he says the apostle seems to see them, feels as if he were there and were looking upon them, and has the same solicitude as if he were present and saw all the danger that their beautiful order and harmony should be disturbed by the influence of false philosophy. The word spirit here does not refer to the Holy Spirit or to any inspiration by which the apostle was enabled to see them, but is equivalent to what we mean when we say, my heart is with you; and he had such confidence that everything would be done among them as became Christians that he could rejoice as if he actually saw it. Ellicott says that to beguile here is to reason into error, and that enticing words are words of persuasion rather than of reason or revelation, both words being used by Paul only in this passage. It would be difficult, he says, to describe more accurately the marvellous fabrics of Gnostic speculation, each step claiming to be based on some fancied probability or metaphysical propriety, but the whole as artificial as the cycles and epicycles of the old Ptolemaic astronomy; we know these in all the elaborate monstrosity of full growth, while Paul doubtless saw them as yet only in embryo. On the next verse he compares the language of 1 Corinthians 5:3 and notes that the word order is used at 1 Corinthians 14:40, while the word stedfastness, or solidity, is not found elsewhere in the New Testament, though the verb from which it derives occurs at Acts 3:7, Acts 3:16 and Acts 16:5 and the original adjective at 1 Peter 5:9. From the days of the ancient Greek interpreters downwards it has been noted that both words have military associations, the one being used for discipline generally and the other for the firm compact solidity of the phalanx, and that the use of them may have been suggested by Paul's captivity under military guard; if both be referred to their faith, the Apostle characterises it as having right order or harmony in its various parts and a strong solidity against all trials. Robertson says Paul explains here why he has made this great claim for Christ at this point in his discussion. The verb rendered delude is an old verb occurring only here in the New Testament, meaning to count aside and so wrong, to cheat by false reckoning, to deceive by false reasoning. The noun rendered persuasiveness of speech is a rare word meaning speech adapted to persuade and then speciously leading astray, also only here in the New Testament, with one papyrus example. The art of persuasion is the height of oratory, but it easily degenerates into trickery and momentary and flashy deceit such as Paul disclaimed at 1 Corinthians 2:4, where he uses the very adjective of which this is another form; and it is curious how winning champions of error, like the Gnostics and modern faddists, can be with a plausibility that catches the gullible. On the next verse Robertson notes the concessive construction and takes order as the military line, unbroken and intact: a few stragglers had gone over to the Gnostics, but there had been no panic, no breach in the line. Steadfastness comes from the verb to make steady and is probably the same military metaphor, the solid part of the line which can and does stand the attack of the Gnostics; he compares Acts 16:5 and 1 Peter 5:9, and notes that at 2 Thessalonians 3 Paul uses the same word of orderly conduct.

Clarke defines both words and reads the second verse as evidence. The first, he says, means to deceive by sophistry or subtle reasoning, in which all the conclusions appear to be fairly drawn from the premises, but the premises are either assumed without evidence or false in themselves; this not being easily discovered, the unthinking or unwary are carried away by the conclusions drawn from them. The second, rendered enticing words, gives the plausible conclusions or deductions from this mode of reasoning, and the apostle seems to allude to the Gentile philosophers, who were notorious for this kind of argumentation, from which Clarke says Plato and Socrates are not free. On the next verse he judges that it is hardly possible such words could have been used to perfect strangers, since they argue a considerable knowledge of the people, and a knowledge founded on personal acquaintance. He notes that the original is exceedingly soft and musical, and that the whole verse shows this Church was sound in doctrine and strict in discipline, having steadfast faith in Christ and regular order among themselves.

debates: Who the enticing words belong to. Clarke lays the method at the door of the Gentile philosophers and does not exempt Plato and Socrates; Barnes names the Greek sophists and rhetoricians; Ellicott and Robertson both point at the Gnostics, Ellicott adding that Paul saw in embryo what later grew monstrous; Henry looks past the agents to Satan himself, the old serpent who beguiled Eve.

Whether the verse implies personal acquaintance. Clarke argues that such words could hardly be addressed to perfect strangers and infer a knowledge founded on acquaintance; Gill takes the opposite view, that Paul had never been corporeally present with them and is anticipating exactly that objection; Barnes takes the presence as affection only and warns that the word spirit means neither the Holy Spirit nor any inspired vision.

What order and stedfastness describe. Ellicott and Robertson hear two military words, discipline and the solidity of the phalanx or line; Calvin takes order morally, for agreement and regulated morals and discipline; Clarke reads the pair as evidence of sound doctrine and strict discipline together.
outliers: Ellicott alone suggests a source for the imagery outside the argument, that the military colouring of both words may have been prompted by the apostle's own captivity under military guard.

Calvin alone turns the sufficiency of Christ into a stated rule of method, that it is not lawful for a Christian to know anything except Christ, and makes every later error a case of aspiring past the simplicity of the gospel.

6.pericope_label: As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him: rooted and built up in him, and stablished in the faith, as ye have been taught, abounding therein with thanksgiving.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the receiving and the roots. Gill says receiving Christ is believing in him: faith is the eye of the soul that sees the beauty, glory, fulness and suitableness of Christ, the foot that goes to him, the hand that takes hold on him and the arm that receives and embraces him, so that this is not a receiving him into the head by notion but into the heart by faith, and not in part only but in whole. Faith receives a whole Christ, his person as God and man, and him in all his offices, as prophet, priest and King, and particularly as a Saviour and Redeemer, a character so exceeding suitable to the case of a sensible sinner; and it receives all the blessings of grace along with him, a justifying righteousness, remission of sins, adoption of children, grace for grace and an inheritance among them that are sanctified, both Christ and these as the free grace gifts of God. On the next verse Gill says believers are sometimes compared to trees, and are trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, whose root is Christ, from whence they spring and by whom they are filled with the fruits of righteousness, deriving all their life, nourishment, fruitfulness, grace and perseverance from him as their root; and they are sometimes compared to a building, a house, a temple, an habitation for God, of which Christ is the sure and only foundation, on which they are laid and where they are safe. Calvin says that to commendation the apostle adds exhortation, teaching them that their having once received Christ will be of no advantage unless they remain in him; and since the false apostles held forth Christ's name with a view to deceive, he obviates the danger by exhorting them to go on as they had received and as they had been taught. They must adhere to the doctrine which they had embraced, as delivered to them by Epaphras, with such constancy as to be on their guard against every other doctrine, according to what Isaiah said, This is the way, walk ye in it; and the truth of the gospel, after it has been manifested to us, must be to us as a brazen wall for keeping back all impostures. The metaphor of the way compares the pure doctrine of the gospel to a road that is sure, so that whoever keeps it is beyond all danger of mistake. The metaphor of the root is taken from trees: as a tree that has struck its roots deep has sufficient support to withstand all the assaults of winds and storms, so one deeply fixed in Christ cannot be thrown down by any machinations of Satan, while one who has not fixed his roots in Christ will easily be carried about with every wind of doctrine, like a tree without a root. The metaphor of the foundation is of the same kind, for a house not supported by a foundation quickly falls to ruins, and so it is with those who lean on any other foundation than Christ, or have the building of their faith suspended as it were in the air. On the next verse Calvin says the apostle repeats without a figure what he had expressed by metaphors, that the prosecution of the way and the support of the root and of the foundation is firmness and steadfastness of faith; he would not have them simply remain immovable but grow every day more and more. In adding the thanksgiving he would have them always keep in mind from what source faith itself proceeds, that they may not be puffed up with presumption but rather with fear repose themselves in the gift of God; and ingratitude, Calvin adds, is very frequently the reason why we are deprived of the light of the gospel as well as of other divine favours.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the reception, the walk and the tenses. Barnes says they had received Christ by faith as their Saviour, or as they were instructed respecting his rank, character and work, and that the object here is to induce them not to swerve from the views they had of Christ when he was made known to them; they had probably received their ideas of the Saviour from the apostle himself, and he means to assure them that those views were founded in truth. To walk in him is to continue in those views, to live in the maintenance of them and to let them regulate the whole conduct; the word walk in the Scriptures denotes the manner of life. The particle so, Barnes notes, is supplied by our translators and rather weakens the sense, and no stress should be laid on it, as is often done; the meaning is simply that since they have received Christ as Lord as he was preached to them, they should hold fast the doctrine received and not permit themselves to be turned aside by any Jewish teachers or teachers of philosophy. On the next verse he says that as a tree strikes its roots deep in the earth, so our faith should strike deep into the doctrine respecting the Saviour; they were established in the faith by the founders of the church and by the faithful ministers who succeeded them, and the thanksgiving is overflowing thanks to God that they have been made acquainted with truths so precious and glorious. Ellicott compares the more emphatic language of the first chapter, and says that as in the case of the Corinthians and the Galatians the apostle entreats them not to be turned aside to another Jesus, or another gospel which is not another. On the next verse he notes a significant change of tense in the original: they had been rooted and grounded in Him once for all, and are being built up continually on that Foundation. Paul bids them seek not only the first basis of their faith but their continual growth in Christ alone, by continual strengthening in the faith which rests in Him; and Ellicott recalls that in the Gnostic teaching faith was held good for the beginner or the common herd, while knowledge was the bright particular jewel of those who went on to perfection. On the thanksgiving he says the metaphor is changed: the cup of faith, filled to the full, runs over in that thanksgiving which is the expression both of faith and love. Robertson notes that the verb rendered received is used in the same sense as at 1 Thessalonians 4:1 and Philippians 4:9, of learning from Epaphras and others, and that the peculiar phrase Christ Jesus the Lord occurs nowhere else in Paul, who has often the Christ, or Jesus Christ, or Christ Jesus, or the Lord Jesus, but nowhere else this combination. Hence it is plain, Robertson judges, that Paul here meets the two forms of Gnostic heresy about the Person of Christ, the recognition of the historical Jesus in his actual humanity against the Docetic Gnostics, and the identity of the Christ or Messiah with this historical Jesus against the Cerinthian Gnostics, together with the acknowledgment of him as Lord: as therefore ye received the Christ, Jesus the Lord. They were taught right. Walk in him he renders, go on walking in him, in the present tense: stick to your first lessons in Christ. On the next verse he notes the perfect passive participle of the verb to root, found in the New Testament only here and at Ephesians 3:17, and says Paul changes the figure from walk to growing tree, rooted to stay so; then the present passive participle of the verb to build upon changes the metaphor again to a building continually going up. Established is a present passive participle of the verb to make firm or stable, and the words even as ye were taught allude back to the receiving of the previous verse and to the learning of the first chapter. Since the walk is in thanksgiving, Robertson concludes, they had no occasion to yield to the blandishments of the Gnostic teachers.

Clarke and Wesley warn off a false emphasis and keep the figures. Clarke says many persons lay a certain stress on the words as and so and make various fine heads of discourse from them, such as, as ye received Christ in a spirit of humility, so walk in him; this may be all proper in itself, but nothing of the kind was intended by the apostle, whose meaning is simply this, that seeing they have embraced the doctrine of Christ they should continue to hold it fast and not permit themselves to be turned aside by sophistical or Judaizing teachers. On the next verse Clarke says it is not usual with the apostle to employ this double metaphor, taken partly from the growth of a tree and partly from the increase of a building: they are to be rooted, and as the good seed had already been sown it is to take root and the roots are to spread far, wide and deep; they are to be grounded, and as the foundation has already been laid they are to build thereon, so that in the one case they bear much fruit and in the other grow up to be a habitation of God through the Spirit. No limitation, he adds, is ever set to the operations of God on the soul, or to the growth of the soul in the knowledge, love and image of God, and those brought into such a state of salvation should abound in gratitude and loving obedience as they grow in grace. Wesley glosses the walk as in the same faith, love and holiness, and the figures as rooted in him, as the vine, and built on the sure foundation.

Chrysostom says the apostle again takes hold on them beforehand with their own testimony, saying, as therefore ye received: we introduce no strange addition, he saith, neither do ye. Walk ye in Him, for He is the Way that leadeth to the Father; not in the Angels, for this way leadeth not thither. Rooted, that is, fixed, not one while going this way and another that, but rooted; and that which is rooted never can remove. Chrysostom bids the reader observe how appropriate are the expressions the apostle employs. And built up, that is, in thought attaining unto Him; and stablished in Him, that is, holding Him, built as on a foundation. He shows that they had fallen down, for the word built has this force; for the faith is in truth a building, and needs both a strong foundation and secure construction, since if any one build not upon a secure foundation it will shake, and even though he do, if it be not firm it will not stand. On the words as ye were taught he again notes the word as. Abounding, he saith, in thanksgiving; for this is the part of well-disposed persons, not simply to give thanks, but with great abundance, more than they had learned, if possible with much ambition.

debates: How much weight the particles will bear. Clarke says preachers make fine heads of discourse from the words as and so which the apostle never intended; Barnes says the word so is the translators' addition and rather weakens the sense, so that no stress should be laid on it; Robertson puts the weight instead on the title Christ Jesus the Lord, which he says occurs nowhere else in Paul.

What the two figures are doing. Chrysostom takes rooted for fixity and built for a fall already suffered, since the word built implies they had fallen down; Clarke notes that joining a tree to a building is unusual for the apostle and keeps the two uses apart, fruit from the one and a habitation of God from the other; Ellicott and Robertson locate the difference in tense, a rooting once for all and a building continually going up; Calvin and Gill use both figures for security against storm and collapse.

What the thanksgiving guards. Ellicott makes it the overflow of a full cup and the expression of faith and love together; Chrysostom asks for more of it than they had been taught; Calvin makes it a guard against presumption and warns that ingratitude often costs men the light of the gospel; Robertson makes it the reason they need not yield to the Gnostic teachers.
outliers: Chrysostom alone turns the walk into a direct denial of the angel-worship the chapter will name later, since Christ is the Way that leads to the Father and the Angels are not.

Ellicott alone explains the pairing of faith and growth from the opposing system, recalling that in Gnostic teaching faith was thought good enough for beginners while knowledge was reserved for those going on to perfection.

8.pericope_label: Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin picture the robbery and defend philosophy rightly understood. Gill says to spoil is to despoil, to rob them of the rich treasure of the Gospel, strip them of their spiritual armour, take away the truths and doctrines of Christ and divest them of their spiritual privileges and blessings, suggesting that the false teachers were thieves and robbers and men of prey; or to drive and carry them away as spoils, as the innocent harmless sheep are driven and carried away by wolves and by the thief that comes to steal, to kill and to destroy. It therefore became them to be upon their guard, to watch, look out and beware lest they should be surprised by these deceitful workers, who lay in wait to deceive and were wolves in sheep's clothing who transformed themselves into the apostles of Christ; and to take heed lest any man hurt them, be he ever so wise and learned, or thought ever so good, religious and sincere, since men of this cast put on such masks and false appearances on purpose to beguile. Calvin says the apostle makes use of a very appropriate term, alluding to thieves who, when they cannot carry off the flock by violence, drive away some of the cattle fraudulently; thus he makes Christ's Church a sheep-fold and the pure doctrine of the gospel the enclosures of the fold, intimating that we who are the sheep of Christ repose in safety when we hold the unity of the faith, while he likens the false apostles to those that carry us away from the folds. Would you be reckoned as belonging to Christ's flock and remain in his folds? Then do not deviate a nail's breadth from purity of doctrine; and the tenth chapter of John, Calvin says, is the exposition of the passage before us. As many have mistakenly imagined that philosophy is here condemned by Paul, Calvin points out what is meant by the term: everything that men contrive of themselves when wishing to be wise through means of their own understanding, and that not without a specious pretext of reason, so as to have a plausible appearance. There is no difficulty in rejecting those contrivances of men which have nothing to set them off, but the difficulty lies in rejecting those that captivate men's minds by a false conceit of wisdom; or, in one word, philosophy of this kind is nothing else than a persuasive speech which insinuates itself into the minds of men by elegant and plausible arguments. Of such a nature, Calvin acknowledges, will all the subtleties of philosophers be if they are inclined to add anything of their own to the pure word of God, and it will be nothing else than a corruption of spiritual doctrine if it is mixed up with Christ; but under the term Paul has merely condemned all spurious doctrines which come forth from man's head, whatever appearance of reason they may have. Calvin adds that Paul convicts this philosophy of vanity on a twofold account, because it is not according to Christ but according to the inclinations of men, and because it consists in the rudiments of the world; and he observes that Christ is placed in opposition to the rudiments equally as to the tradition, by which Paul intimates that whatever is hatched in man's brain is not in accordance with Christ, who has been appointed us by the Father as our sole Teacher, that he might retain us in the simplicity of his gospel, which is corrupted by even a small portion of that leaven. All doctrines are foreign to Christ, Calvin concludes, that make the worship of God, which we know to be spiritual, consist in the visible things of this world, and that fetter the minds of men by such trifles and frivolities, while Christ calls us directly to himself.

Henry distinguishes two philosophies. There is a philosophy which rightly exercises our reasonable faculties, a study of the works of God which leads us to the knowledge of God and confirms our faith in him; but there is a philosophy which is vain and deceitful, and which, while it pleases men's fancies, hinders their faith, such as curious speculations about things above us or of no concern to us. Those who walk in the way of the world, Henry adds, are turned from following Christ.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson define the verb and locate the danger. Barnes says the word spoil now commonly means to corrupt, to cause to decay and perish, as fruit is spoiled by keeping too long or hay by a long rain, but the Greek word here used means to spoil in the sense of plunder or rob, as when plunder is taken in war: take heed lest any one plunder or rob you of your faith and hope by philosophy, for these false teachers would strip them of faith and hope as an invading army would rob a country of all that was valuable. The Greek philosophy prevailed much in the regions around Colosse, and perhaps also the Oriental or Gnostic philosophy, and they were exposed to the influence of these plausible systems, which consisted much of speculations respecting the nature of the Divine existence; the danger was that they would rely rather on the deductions of that specious reasoning than on what they had been taught by their Christian teachers. Vain deceit is mere fallacy: the doctrines advanced in those systems were maintained by plausible, not solid, arguments, fitted not to lead to the truth but to lead astray. Barnes distinguishes two sources of danger to which the Colossians were exposed, one arising from the Grecian philosophy and the other from Jewish opinions, and refers the tradition of men to the latter, since the Jews depended much on tradition and many of those traditions would have tended to corrupt the gospel of Christ. Not after Christ means not such as Christ taught. Ellicott says the word means properly to lead you away as a spoil, to triumph over you as a captive and make you a slave, and compares Paul's language about the older Judaism at Corinth. Philosophy and vain deceit means, like the knowledge falsely so called of 1 Timothy 6:20, a philosophy inseparably connected with vain deceit, and the warning is two-fold. First, against considering Christianity primarily as a philosophy, that is a search for and knowledge of speculative truth, even the highest: that it involves philosophy is obvious, since it claims to solve the great problem of Being in Nature, in Man and in God, and Paul, while depreciating the wisdom of this world, dwells emphatically on the gospel as the wisdom of God and speaks of wisdom again and again in this Epistle as a great characteristic of Christian life; nor is it less clear, as the ancient Greek commentators earnestly remind us, that Christianity finds a place and a blessing for all true philosophy of men and makes it, as Paul made it at Athens, an introduction to the higher wisdom. But Christianity is not a philosophy but a life, not a knowledge of abstract principles but a personal knowledge of faith and love of God in Christ. Second, against accepting in philosophy the vain deceit of mere speculation and imagination instead of the modest, laborious investigation of facts: this is the knowledge falsely so called, of which it may be said that it puffs up and does not build up, and which in ancient and modern times has always confused brilliant theory with solid discovery, delighting especially to dissolve the great facts of the gospel into abstractions. The tradition of men is the keynote of our Lord's condemnation of the old Pharisaic exclusiveness and formalism, and equally the condemnation of the later Jewish or half-Jewish mysticism which Paul attacks here; the Apostle often claims reverence for traditions, but they are traditions having their starting point in direct revelation of God and freely given to all as being His, whereas the traditions of men here condemned had their origin in human speculation and were secretly transmitted to the initiated only. The rudiments of the world mark the chief point of contact with the earlier Judaism, in the stress still laid on matters of ritual, law and ascetic observance; these are of the world, that is belonging to the visible sphere, and they are rudiments, fit only for the elementary education of those who are as children and intended simply as preparation for a higher teaching. Robertson takes the opening verb as a common word for warning, like our look out, and notes that the participle rendered that maketh spoil of you is from a late and rare verb, found here first, from booty and to lead, meaning to carry off as booty a captive, slave or maiden, and occurring only here in the New Testament. He notes the singular: there was some one outstanding leader who was doing most of the damage in leading the people astray. Philosophy is the only use of the word in the New Testament and is employed by Paul because the Gnostics were fond of it; Paul does not condemn knowledge and wisdom, but only this false philosophy, knowledge falsely named, explained here by the next words. Vain deceit is an old word for trick or guile. Tradition is a giving over, a passing on, and the word is colourless in itself: the tradition may be good or bad, and here it is worthless and harmful, merely the foolish theories of the Gnostics. Rudiments is an old word for anything in a row or series, like the letters of the alphabet, used of the materials of the universe, of elementary teaching, of the elements of Jewish ceremonial training, and here of the specious arguments of the Gnostic philosophers with all their aeons and rules of life. Christ, Robertson concludes, is the yardstick by which to measure philosophy and all phases of human knowledge; the Gnostics were measuring Christ by their philosophy, as many men are doing today, and they have it backwards, since Christ is the measure for all human knowledge, being the Creator and Sustainer of the universe.

Clarke and Wesley identify the philosophy as Jewish and shallow. Clarke says the word signifies to rob or spoil of their goods as if by violence or rapine, being formed from prey and to lead or carry away; their goods were the salvation they had received from Christ, and both the Gentile and Jewish teachers endeavoured to deprive them of these by perverting their minds and leading them off from the truths of Christianity. He renders the next phrase as the vain or empty deceit of philosophy, such philosophizing as the Jewish and Gentile teachers used; and since the term philosophy stood in high repute among the Gentiles, the Jews of that time affected it, both Philo and Josephus using the word to express the whole of the Mosaic institutions, the one speaking of those who embraced the philosophy of Moses and the other of three systems of philosophy among the Jews, meaning the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes. The Jewish philosophy such as is found in the Cabala and the Midrashim, Clarke says, deserves the character of vain deceit in the fullest sense of the words, the inspired writers excepted; and even Maimonides, the most intelligent of them all, is often in his masterpiece most deplorably empty and vain. The rudiments of the world Clarke takes according to the doctrine of the Jewish teachers, or the Mosaic institutions as explained and glossed by the scribes, Pharisees and rabbins in general, noting that the Hebrew phrase for this world is frequently used to express the Jewish system of rites, ceremonies and institutions in general, which the apostle calls the tradition of men, namely what men unauthorized by God have taught as doctrines received from him, and which our Lord frequently condemns. Not after Christ means not according to the simple doctrine of Christ, that he died for our offences, and that believing on the Lord Jesus one shall be saved. Wesley reads the phrase as the empty deceit of philosophy blended with Christianity, and condemns it on three grounds: because it was empty and deceitful, promising happiness but giving none; because it was grounded not on solid reason but on the traditions of men, Zeno, Epicurus and the rest; and because it was so shallow and superficial, not advancing beyond the knowledge of sensible things, no, not beyond the first rudiments of them.

Cyril joins right doctrine to right practice and names the deceivers. The method of godliness, he says, consists of these two things, pious doctrines and virtuous practice: neither are the doctrines acceptable to God apart from good works, nor does God accept the works which are not perfected with pious doctrines. For what profit is it to know well the doctrines concerning God and yet to be a vile fornicator? And again, what profit is it to be nobly temperate and an impious blasphemer? A most precious possession, therefore, is the knowledge of doctrines; and there is need also of a wakeful soul, since there are many that make spoil through philosophy and vain deceit. The Greeks on the one hand draw men away by their smooth tongue; they of the Circumcision deceive those who come to them by means of the Divine Scriptures, which they miserably misinterpret though studying them from childhood to old age and growing old in ignorance; and the children of heretics, by their good words and smooth tongue, deceive the hearts of the innocent, disguising with the name of Christ, as it were with honey, the poisoned arrows of their impious doctrines.

debates: Whether philosophy itself is condemned. Calvin says many have mistakenly imagined so, and restricts the condemnation to what men contrive of themselves under a specious pretext of reason; Henry allows one philosophy that leads to the knowledge of God and condemns another that pleases men's fancies; Ellicott holds that Christianity finds a place and a blessing for all true philosophy and made it at Athens an introduction to the higher wisdom, while itself being a life and not a philosophy; Robertson says Paul condemns not knowledge but knowledge falsely named.

Where the false teaching came from. Barnes finds two sources, Grecian philosophy and Jewish opinion, referring the tradition of men to the second; Clarke makes it almost wholly Jewish and cites Philo and Josephus using the word philosophy of the Mosaic institutions; Robertson and Ellicott read the whole passage against the Gnostics; Wesley names the Greek schools of Zeno and Epicurus; Cyril, earliest of them, names Greeks, the Circumcision and heretics together.

How the tradition of men differs from tradition the apostle honours. Ellicott says the traditions Paul elsewhere claims reverence for begin in direct revelation and are freely given to all, while these began in human speculation and were secretly transmitted to the initiated only; Robertson says the word is colourless in itself and may be good or bad; Clarke defines it as what men unauthorized by God have taught as doctrines received from him.
outliers: Robertson alone reads the grammar as evidence about the situation, noting that the participle is singular and inferring that one outstanding leader was doing most of the damage at Colosse.
Cyril alone makes the passage a test of life as well as of doctrine, holding that sound doctrine without good works and good works without sound doctrine are alike unacceptable to God.
themes: beware lest any man spoil you

9.pericope_label: For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the indwelling and the completeness. Gill says the words are to be understood not of the doctrine or Gospel of Christ as a perfect revelation of the will of God, but of Christ, and particularly of his human nature, as consisting of a true body and a reasonable soul, in which the Godhead dwells in a most eminent manner. God is everywhere by his powerful presence, was in the tabernacle and temple in a very singular manner and dwells in the saints in a way of special grace, but resides in the human nature of Christ in the highest and most exalted manner; that nature is to deity what the human body is to a human soul, the house in which it dwells, and Gill notes that Philo the Jew calls the Logos the house of God. The Godhead dwells in Christ as in a tabernacle, in allusion to the tabernacle of Moses, which looked mean outside but glorious within, where God granted his presence and accepted the sacrifices of his people. On the next verse Gill renders it filled up or filled full, and says the words are not an exhortation to perfection, as the Arabic version reads them, but an affirmation, asserting not what the saints shall be hereafter or in heaven but what they now are, and that not in themselves, for in themselves none are perfect, not even those who are truly sanctified. Though all grace is seminally implanted in them and they have a perfection of parts, and are perfect in comparison of what they once were and of profane persons and hypocrites and with respect to weaker believers, yet none are absolutely perfect: the good work of grace is not yet finished in them, sin dwells in them, they are full of wants and complaints, and the best of them disclaim perfection as attained by them and express their desires of it. Calvin says here we have the reason why the doctrines taught by men do not accord with Christ, namely that they are additions for supplying a deficiency; but in Christ there is a perfection to which nothing can be added, so that everything mankind of themselves mix up is at variance with Christ's nature, because it charges him with imperfection. This argument of itself, he says, will suffice for setting aside all the contrivances of the Papists, who allege that they add nothing to Christ since what they have appended to the gospel is as it were a part of Christianity, but who do not escape by a cavil of that kind, since Paul speaks not of an imaginary Christ but of a Christ preached, who has revealed himself by express doctrine. When Paul says the fulness dwells in Christ he means simply that God is wholly found in him, so that whoever is not contented with Christ alone desires something better and more excellent than God; the sum is that God has manifested himself to us fully and perfectly in Christ. Calvin says interpreters explain the adverb in different ways and that for his own part he has no doubt it is employed not in a strict sense, and he sets this manifestation of God against all others that have ever been made: God has often manifested himself to men, but only in part, and otherwise in figures or by power and grace, whereas in Christ he communicates himself wholly and has appeared to us essentially, so that the statement of John holds good, that he who has the Son has the Father also. On the next verse Calvin says this perfect essence of Deity in Christ is profitable to us in this respect, that we also are perfect in him; those who do not rest satisfied with Christ alone do injury to God in two ways, detracting from his glory by desiring something above his perfection, and being ungrateful in seeking elsewhere what they already have in Christ. Paul does not mean that the perfection of Christ is transfused into us, but that there are in him resources from which we may be filled, that nothing may be wanting to us; and he has introduced the clause about the head again on account of the angels, meaning that the angels also will be ours if we have Christ. We are hemmed in, Calvin says, above and below with railings, that our faith may not deviate even to the slightest extent from Christ.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson define the terms and answer the opponents. Barnes says this was the great and central doctrine to be maintained about Christ, and that almost all heresy has begun by some form of the denial of the great central truth of the incarnation of the Son of God. The word rendered Godhead properly denotes the Divine nature and perfections and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; the word rendered bodily is also found nowhere else, though the adjective occurs twice, and means having a bodily appearance instead of existing or appearing in a spiritual form, so that the fair sense is that the fulness of the Divine nature became incarnate and was indwelling in the body of the Redeemer. It does not meet the case to say, as Crellius does, that the whole Divine will was in him, for the word does not mean the will of God, and it is as certainly true that the inspired prophets were under the control of the Divine will as that the Saviour was; nor can it mean, as Socinus supposes, that the fulness of Divine knowledge dwelt in him, nor that a fulness of Divine gifts was entrusted to him, for the same reason. The language is such as would obviously be employed on the supposition that God became incarnate and appeared in human form, and no other idea can be made to express it without a forced construction: it was not any one attribute of the Deity that became incarnate, but the whole Deity, and no language could more clearly demonstrate the divinity of Christ, since of no mere man and of no angel could it be used. On the next verse Barnes says they had no need, for the purposes of salvation, of any aid from the philosophy of the Greeks or the traditions of the Jews: there is a completion or a filling up in Christ so as to leave nothing wanting, in respect to the wisdom needful to guide us, the atonement to be made for sin, the merit by which a sinner can be justified, and the grace needful to sustain us in the trials and aid us in the duties of life. There is no necessity to look to philosophy as if there were a defect in the teachings of the Saviour, or to human strength as if he were unable to save us, or to the merits of the saints as if those of the Redeemer were not sufficient; and the sentiment of the verse, Barnes adds, would overthrow the whole papal doctrine of the merits of the saints and, of course, the whole doctrine of papal indulgences. Ellicott says that here almost every word is emphatic: first, all the fulness of the Godhead, not a mere emanation from the Supreme Being; next, dwells and remains for ever, not descending on Him for a time and leaving Him again; lastly, bodily, that is as incarnate in His humanity. The whole is an extension and enforcement of the first chapter, and the emphasis is explained by the opponents, since horror of all that was material, as having in it the seed of evil, induced denial either of the reality of our Lord's body or of its inseparable connection with the Godhead in Him, as we find John insisting somewhat later that the Word was made flesh and that the spirit which confesses not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is the spirit of antichrist. On the word fulness Ellicott adds that, as in the later Gnosticism so probably in its earlier forms, the word was used for the infinite nature of the Supreme Deity, out of which all the emanations afterwards called aeons received in various degrees of imperfection according to their capacity, and that Paul probably uses it so emphatically for that reason; it is not finite but infinitely perfect, hence we all can draw from it yet leave it unimpaired. On the next verse he renders it literally, ye have been filled up in His fulness, and says that to partake of the divine fulness is not the special privilege of the initiated but belongs to all who are united to the Lord Jesus Christ; the headship over all angelic natures is dwelt upon, as in Hebrews, with obvious reference to the worshipping of angels, since they are our fellowservants under the same Head. Robertson says that in this sentence, given as the reason for the preceding claim for Christ as the measure of human knowledge, Paul states the heart of his message about the Person of Christ. There dwells at home in Christ not one or more aspects of the Godhead: the word used is the very essence of God, not to be confused with the different word at Romans 1:20 which means the quality of God, each occurring only once in the New Testament, the distinction being observed in Lucian and Plutarch. Paul asserts that all the fulness of the Godhead, not just certain aspects, dwells in Christ, and in bodily form, by a late and rare adverb found in Plutarch and in an inscription and only here in the New Testament; it dwells now in Christ in his glorified humanity, the body of his glory. The fulness of the Godhead was in Christ before the Incarnation and during the Incarnation, and it was the Son of God who came in the likeness of men. Paul here disposes of the Docetic theory that Jesus had no human body as well as the Cerinthian separation between the man Jesus and the aeon Christ, asserting plainly the deity and the humanity of Jesus Christ in corporeal form. On the next verse Robertson notes the periphrastic perfect passive and says Christ is our fulness of which we all partake, our goal being to be made full of God in Christ; in Christ they find the satisfaction of every spiritual want. There is no other place for Christ, who is first in time and in rank, and all rule and authority comes after Christ, whether angels, aeons, kings, or what not.

Clarke and Wesley define the two adverbs and object to the English word complete. Clarke says the fulness in Christ is opposed to the empty doctrine of the Gentile and Jewish philosophers: there is a fulness in Christ suited to the empty, destitute state of the human soul, and no substitute for the grace of the Lord Jesus has ever been found, those who sought one having disquieted themselves in vain. By the Godhead we are to understand the state or being of the Divine nature, and by the fulness of that Deity the infinite attributes essential to such a nature. The word rendered bodily, he says, signifies truly, really, in opposition to typically and figuratively: there was a symbol of the Divine presence in the Hebrew tabernacle and in the Jewish temple, but in the body of Christ the Deity, with all its plenitude of attributes, dwelt really and substantially, and so it was understood by the ancient Greek fathers; the fulness of the Godhead dwelt in Christ bodily as opposed to the Jewish tabernacle or temple, truly and really in opposition to types and figures, not only effectively as God dwells in good men but substantially or personally, by the strictest union, as the soul dwells in the body, so that God and man are one Christ. On the next verse Clarke says our word complete quite destroys the connection subsisting in the apostle's ideas: the philosophy of the world was empty, but there was a fulness in Christ; the Colossians were empty, spoiled and deprived of every good while following the empty philosophy and groundless traditions of Jewish and Gentile teachers, but since they had received Christ Jesus they were filled with him, which is the true meaning of the word. No fanciful completeness in Christ, of a believer while incomplete in himself, Clarke insists, is either expressed or intended by St Paul; it is too bad a doctrine to exist in the oracles of God. Wesley glosses the dwelling as inhabiting and continually abiding, and says believers are filled with all the fulness of God, but in Christ dwells all the fulness of the Godhead, the most full Godhead, not only divine powers but divine nature; bodily means personally, really, substantially, the very substance of God dwelling in Christ in the most full sense. On the next verse Wesley says Christ is filled with God and believers are filled with Christ, and filled by him: the fulness of Christ overflows his church, he being originally full, and we are filled by him with wisdom and holiness. Since he is the head of all principality and power, of angels as well as men, it is not from angels therefore but from their head that we are to ask whatever we stand in need of.

debates: Whether a believer is complete in Christ while incomplete in himself. Clarke denies it flatly, calling such a completeness fanciful, neither expressed nor intended by the apostle, and too bad a doctrine to exist in the oracles of God; Gill affirms very nearly that position, holding the words an affirmation of what saints now are, yet granting that in themselves none are perfect, since the work of grace is unfinished and the best disclaim perfection; Calvin steers between, denying that Christ's perfection is transfused into us and holding only that there are resources in him from which we may be filled.

What the word fulness is doing. Ellicott says it was the opponents' own term for the infinite nature of the Supreme Deity from which the aeons emanated, and that Paul takes it up deliberately; Calvin argues instead from perfection, that anything added to Christ charges him with a deficiency; Barnes and Robertson use it to assert the whole Deity incarnate rather than any single attribute.

What error the word bodily excludes. Clarke sets it against types and figures, the tabernacle and the temple; Ellicott sets it against the horror of matter that denied our Lord a real body; Robertson names the Docetic denial of the body and the Cerinthian separation of Jesus from the Christ; Gill and Wesley take it of a substantial and personal indwelling.
outliers: Barnes alone answers named opponents on the word Godhead, refusing both the reading of Crellius that the Divine will was in Christ and that of Socinus that the fulness of Divine knowledge was, on the ground that the word means neither.

Robertson alone rests the point on a single-letter distinction between two Greek words, this one for the essence of God and the one at Romans 1:20 for the quality of God, noting that the distinction is kept by Lucian and Plutarch.
themes: head of all principality and power
not from angels but from their head

11.pericope_label: In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ: buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin give the occasion and the efficacy. Gill says the words are meant to prevent an objection that might be made to the perfection of these Gentile believers, because they were not circumcised, for the Jews thought that perfection lay in circumcision, or at least that there could be no perfection without it. On the next verse Gill says the apostle goes on to observe how complete the saints are in Christ: they are not only circumcised in him in a spiritual sense, and the body of the sins of their flesh put off and removed, in allusion to the cutting off and casting away of the foreskin, but they and all their sins were buried with Christ, of which their baptism in water was a lively representation. Christ, having died for their sins, was laid in the grave, where he continued for a while and then rose again; and as they were crucified with him they were also buried with him, as their head and representative, and all their sins too, which he left behind him in the grave. Baptism being performed by immersion, when the person baptized is covered with water and as it were buried in it, is a very significant emblem of all this, and a representation of the burial of Christ. Calvin says it appears from this that Paul has a controversy with the false apostles, who mixed the law with the gospel and by that means made Christ have as it were two faces; he specifies one instance by way of example, and proves that the circumcision of Moses is not merely unnecessary but opposed to Christ, because it destroys the spiritual reality. Circumcision was given to the Fathers that it might be the figure of a thing that was absent, and those who retain that figure after Christ's advent deny the accomplishment of what it prefigured; outward circumcision is here compared with spiritual as a figure with the reality, and the figure is of a thing absent, so that where the reality exists the shadowy emblem vanishes. Calvin says the term body is employed by an elegant metaphor to denote a mass made up of all vices: as we are encompassed by our bodies, so we are surrounded on all sides by an accumulation of vices, and as the body is composed of various members, each of which has its own actings and offices, so from that accumulation of corruption all sins take their rise as members of the entire body. It is Christ who circumcises the foreskin of our heart, mortifying all the lusts of the flesh not with the knife but by his Spirit, so that in him is the reality of the figure. On the next verse Calvin says Paul explains still more clearly the manner of spiritual circumcision, because, being buried with Christ, we are partakers of his death, and he expressly declares that we obtain this by means of baptism, so that it may be more clearly apparent that there is no advantage from circumcision under the reign of Christ. Someone might object: why abolish circumcision on the pretext that its accomplishment is in Christ, when Abraham also was circumcised spiritually and yet this did not hinder the adding of the sign to the reality? Paul anticipates that objection by making mention of baptism: Christ accomplishes in us spiritual circumcision, not by means of that ancient sign which was in force under Moses, but by baptism, which is therefore the sign of the thing presented to us, prefigured while absent by circumcision. When Paul says that we are buried, this means more than that we are dead with Christ, for burial expresses a continued process of mortification; and in saying that this is done by means of baptism he speaks in his usual manner, ascribing efficacy to the sacrament, that it may not fruitlessly signify what does not exist. By baptism, therefore, we are buried, because Christ at the same time accomplishes efficaciously that mortification which he there represents, that the reality may be conjoined with the sign. Calvin adds that faith is founded upon the power of God; but as faith does not wander in a confused and undefined contemplation of divine power, Paul intimates what it ought to have in view, namely that by which God raised Christ from the dead.
