He takes it for granted that, since it is impossible that believers should be severed from their head, the same power of God which shewed itself in Christ is diffused among them all in common.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the phrases and the rite. Barnes says the meaning is that in connexion with Christ they have received what was designed to be represented by circumcision, the putting away of sin, that made in the heart by the renunciation of all sin. The Jewish teachers insisted on the necessity of literal circumcision in order to salvation, and hence the subject is so often introduced into the writings of Paul, who is at pains to show that by believing in Christ all was obtained that was required for salvation. Circumcision was an ordinance denoting that all sin was to be cut off or renounced and that he who was circumcised was to be devoted to God and to a holy life; all this was obtained by the gospel, and what Christians obtained related to the heart and was not a mere ordinance pertaining to the flesh. The word body here seems used with reference to circumcision: in that ordinance the body of the flesh was subjected to the rite, while with Christians it is the body of sin that is cut off. By the circumcision of Christ means not that Christ was circumcised but that we have the kind of circumcision which Christ established, the renouncing of sin; and since we have thus been enabled to renounce sin and devote ourselves to God, we should not be induced by plausible arguments to return to an ordinance pertaining to the flesh as if it were needful for salvation. On the next verse Barnes takes the rising as from the death of sin to the life of religion, and the faith as a firm belief in the agency of God in raising Christ up; the resurrection of Christ is often represented as the foundation of all our hopes, and as he was raised to die no more, so in virtue of that we are raised from the death of sin to eternal spiritual life. The belief of this is shown by our baptism, Barnes adds, whatever be the mode in which the ordinance is performed, and is as well shown in one mode as another. Ellicott says the abrupt introduction of circumcision would be difficult to understand were it not for the enforcement of Jewish observance so strangely mixed with this philosophy at Colossae. The phrase made without hands is so constantly used of heavenly realities, as opposed to earthly symbols, that it comes to have the positive sense of spiritual, and it is defined below as the circumcision of Christ, that which Christ has given us in Himself, in contradistinction to the old circumcision which is now nothing. The words of the sins are not found in the best manuscripts and are no doubt an explanatory gloss to soften the harshness of the phrase the body of the flesh. What the body of the flesh is we see clearly from the third chapter, where the old man is put off: it is, like the body of sin at Romans 6:6 and the body of death at Romans 7:24, the body so far as it is, in the bad sense of the word flesh, fleshly. The body itself is not put off, for it is not evil; it is a part of the true man and becomes the temple of God, and it is only so far as in it the flesh rebels against the spirit that it is to be put off. But why the body of the flesh and not the flesh simply? The answer, Ellicott says, is that the bodily circumcision was but of one member, in mere symbolism of one form of purity, while the spiritual circumcision is the putting away of the whole of the power of the flesh, and that not in symbol but in reality. On the next verse he compares Romans 6:4, where the former clause is identical while the latter is here stronger: what in the earlier Epistle is the likeness of His Resurrection is here the participation of it, and instead of a simple allusion to Christ's being raised we have faith in the operation of God who raised Him. The energy of the mighty power of God is conceived as actually working both in the Head and in the Body, so that we through it partake of the resurrection, the ascension and the glorified majesty of Christ, which shows an instructive development in this Epistle of the consequences of union with Christ. The passage is also notable for the obvious contrast of baptism, as a spiritual reality, with circumcision as a symbolic form: each is the entrance into a covenant with God, but the one into a covenant of the letter and the other into a covenant of the spirit; and baptism, being always looked upon as the means of spiritual regeneration, is brought out emphatically as the circumcision of the Spirit. Robertson says the verb is used here as a metaphor in a spiritual sense, as in the circumcision of the heart at Romans 2:29. The word rendered not made with hands is a late and rare negative compound verbal occurring only in the New Testament, formed by merely adding the alpha privative to the old verbal made with hands, and possibly first at Mark 14:58, where both words occur concerning the temple. The word for the putting off is as of an old garment, the fleshly body, and occurs nowhere else so far as known, being made in a perfectly normal way by the perfective use of two Greek prepositions; Paul had as much right to mint a Greek compound as any one, and surely no one ever had more ideas to express or more power in doing it. Of Christ is a specifying genitive, the kind of circumcision that belongs to Christ, that of the heart. On the next verse Robertson notes the second aorist passive participle of the verb to bury together, found in the New Testament only here and at Romans 6:4, and quotes the lexicon that all who in the rite of baptism are plunged under the water thereby declare that they put faith in the expiatory death of Christ for the pardon of their past sins, adding, yes, and for all future sins also. The word gives Paul's vivid picture of baptism as a symbolic burial with Christ and resurrection also to newness of life in him, and in the symbol the resurrection to new life is pictured with an allusion to Christ's own resurrection and to our final resurrection. But Paul does not mean to say that the new life in Christ is caused or created by the act of baptism; that is grossly to misunderstand him. The Gnostics and the Judaizers were sacramentalists, but not so Paul, the champion of spiritual Christianity, who has just given the spiritual interpretation to circumcision which itself followed Abraham's faith: baptism gives a picture of the change already wrought in the heart through faith. God had power to raise Christ from the dead, and he has power to give us new life in Christ by faith.

Clarke and Wesley take the spiritual rite and the mode of baptism. Clarke says all that was designed by circumcision literally performed is accomplished in them that believe, through the Spirit and power of Christ: it is not a cutting off of a part of the flesh but a putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, the law requiring the circumcision of the flesh and the Gospel of Christ the circumcision of the heart. He notes that the words of the sins are omitted by many manuscripts, by several versions and by several of the fathers, and that Griesbach has omitted them. On the next verse Clarke says the burial alludes to the immersions practised in the case of adults, wherein the person appeared to be buried under the water as Christ was buried in the heart of the earth; his rising again the third day, and their emerging from the water, was an emblem of the resurrection of the body and, in them, of a total change of life. They were quickened, changed and saved by means of faith in Christ Jesus, which faith was produced by the operation or energy of God: believing is the act of the soul, but the grace or power to believe comes from God himself. Wesley says they have received the spiritual blessings typified of old by circumcision, by an inward, spiritual operation, putting off not a little skin but the whole body of the sins of the flesh, all the sins of their evil nature, by that spiritual circumcision which Christ works in the heart. On the next verse Wesley says the ancient manner of baptizing by immersion is as manifestly alluded to here as the other manner by sprinkling or pouring of water is at Hebrews 10:22, but that no stress is laid on the age of the baptized, or the manner of performing it, in one or the other, only on our being risen with Christ through the powerful operation of God in the soul, which we cannot but know assuredly if it really is so; and if we do not experience this, our baptism has not answered the end of its institution. He adds that it does not appear that in all this the apostle speaks of justification at all, but of sanctification altogether.

Cyril traces the sonship of Abraham to faith and the seal to baptism. Of Jews, he says, Abraham is confessedly the father through succession according to the flesh; but if we hold to the succession according to the flesh we shall be compelled to say that the oracle calling him father of many nations was false, for according to the flesh he is no longer father of us all. It is the example of his faith that makes us all sons of Abraham. With men it is incredible that one should rise from the dead, as in like manner it is incredible that there should be offspring from aged persons as good as dead; but when Christ is preached as having been crucified on the tree, and as having died and risen again, we believe it, and by the likeness of our faith we are adopted into the sonship of Abraham. Then, following upon our faith, we receive like him the spiritual seal, being circumcised by the Holy Spirit through Baptism, not in the foreskin of the body but in the heart, according to Jeremiah, who said that they should be circumcised unto God in the foreskin of their heart.

debates: Whether the words of the sins belong to the text. Clarke reports them omitted by many manuscripts, versions and fathers and dropped by Griesbach; Ellicott says they are absent from the best copies and are an explanatory gloss added to soften the harshness of the phrase the body of the flesh; the others read the longer text without comment.

Whether the mode of baptism is being taught. Clarke and Gill both read immersion out of the burial, Clarke pointing to the immersions practised in the case of adults and Gill calling the covering with water a very significant emblem; Wesley grants the allusion but insists that no stress is laid on either the age of the baptized or the manner, only on being risen with Christ; Barnes says the belief is as well shown in one mode as another.

What baptism effects. Robertson denies that the new life is caused or created by the act, calls the contrary a gross misunderstanding, and sets Paul against the Gnostics and Judaizers as sacramentalists, baptism giving a picture of a change already wrought; Calvin ascribes efficacy to the sacrament, so that it may not fruitlessly signify what does not exist, holding that Christ accomplishes at the same time the mortification the sign represents.

Why the phrase is the body of the flesh. Ellicott answers that the bodily rite touched one member only, in symbolism of one form of purity, while the spiritual circumcision puts away the whole power of the flesh in reality; Calvin takes body as a metaphor for a mass of vices with members of its own; Barnes keeps the comparison with the rite, the body of flesh subjected there and the body of sin cut off here.
outliers: Robertson alone pauses on Paul's word-making, observing that the noun for the putting off occurs nowhere else and was probably coined for the occasion, and defending the apostle's right to mint a Greek compound.
Wesley alone marks what the passage does not treat, judging that the apostle is not speaking of justification here at all but of sanctification altogether.
themes: the body of the sins of the flesh

13.pericope_label: And you, being dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, hath he quickened together with him, having forgiven you all trespasses; blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin describe the death and the ceremonies. Gill says they were dead not corporeally, though sin had subjected them to a corporeal death, but morally: sin had brought a death upon them in a moral sense, they were separated from God as at death the body is from the soul, and so were alienated from the life of God. They had lost the image of God, which consisted in knowledge, righteousness and holiness, and were dead as to the understanding of what was good, as to their affections for it and their will and capacity to do it; like dead men they were insensible of their state, their sin and their misery, and altogether inactive and helpless in spiritual things, being destitute of spiritual life, strength and motion, and were in themselves deserving of eternal death and, according to the law of works, under the sentence of it. On the next verse Gill reports the various senses interpreters give: some think the handwriting means the covenant God made with Adam, which being broken obliged him and all his posterity to the penalty of death but is cancelled by Christ; others the agreement the Israelites made at Mount Sinai when they said, all that the Lord hath said will we do and be obedient, which was as it were setting their hands and laying themselves under obligation to obedience and, in case of failure, to the penalty of the law; others God's book of remembrance of the sins of men, out of which they are blotted when pardoned; others the book of conscience, which bears witness to every violation of the law and may be said to be blotted out when pacified with an application of the blood and righteousness of Christ. Rather, with others, Gill says it signifies the ceremonial law, which lay in divers ordinances and commands, and is what the apostle afterwards speaks of more clearly and particularly. Calvin says the apostle admonishes the Colossians to recognize as applicable to themselves what he had treated in a general way, which is by far the most effectual way of teaching; and since they were Gentiles when converted to Christ, he takes occasion to show how absurd it is to pass over from Christ to the ceremonies of Moses. The term uncircumcision may be understood either in its proper signification or figuratively. Taken properly, the meaning will be that uncircumcision is the badge of alienation from God, for where the covenant of grace is not there is pollution and consequently curse and ruin, but God has called them to himself from uncircumcision and therefore from death; so that uncircumcision is represented not as the cause of death but as a token that they were estranged from God. Taken metaphorically, there would be an allusion to natural uncircumcision, but Paul would be speaking of the obstinacy of the human heart in opposition to God and of a nature defiled by corrupt affections. Calvin prefers the former exposition, because it corresponds better with the context, since Paul declares that uncircumcision was no hindrance in the way of their becoming partakers of Christ's life, from which it follows that circumcision derogated from the grace of God which they had already obtained. It is customary in Scripture, he adds, to denote deprivation of the reality by deprivation of the sign, as in Genesis, lest Adam eat of the fruit of life and live, for the tree did not confer life, but its being taken away was a sign of death. On the next verse Calvin says the apostle now contends with the false apostles in close combat, for this was the main point in question, whether the observance of ceremonies was necessary under the reign of Christ. Paul contends that ceremonies have been abolished, and to prove it he compares them to a handwriting by which God holds us bound, that we may not be able to deny our guilt; we have been freed from condemnation in such a manner that even the handwriting is effaced, that no remembrance of it might remain. As to debts, the obligation is still in force so long as the handwriting remains, and by the erasing or tearing of the handwriting the debtor is set free; hence all who still urge the observance of ceremonies detract from the grace of Christ, as though absolution were not procured through him, for they restore to the handwriting its freshness so as to hold us still under obligation. Calvin rejects the view of those who think Paul speaks simply of the moral law, since Paul is accustomed to give that name to the department which consists in ceremonies, and does better with those who restrict it to ceremonies, though they too err in not adding the true reason why it is a handwriting. The reason is that all the ceremonies of Moses had in them some acknowledgment of guilt, which bound those that observed them with a firmer tie in the view of God's judgment: what else were washings than an evidence of pollution, and whenever a victim was sacrificed did not the people that stood by behold in it a representation of his death, since in substituting an innocent animal in their place they confessed that they were themselves deserving of that death? In proportion as there were ceremonies belonging to it, just so many exhibitions were there of human guilt and of obligation.

Henry sets out the privileges Christians have above the Jews. A state of sin, he says, is a state of spiritual death: as the death of the body consists in its separation from the soul, so the death of the soul consists in its separation from God and the divine favour; as the death of the body is its corruption and putrefaction, so sin is the corruption or depravation of the soul; and as a man who is dead is unable to help himself by any power of his own, so an habitual sinner is morally impotent, having a natural power, or the power of a reasonable creature, but not a spiritual power until he has the divine life or a renewed nature. It is principally to be understood of the Gentile world, who lay in wickedness, being aliens to the covenant of promise and without God in the world. Henry distinguishes two deaths: dead in law, as a condemned malefactor is called a dead man because he is under a sentence of death, so sinners by the guilt of sin are under the sentence of the law and condemned already; and dead in state, by reason of the uncircumcision of our flesh, an unsanctified heart being called an uncircumcised heart. Now through Christ we who were dead in sins are quickened, that is, effectual provision is made for taking away the guilt of sin and breaking the power and dominion of it, and this by virtue of our union to him and in conformity to him: Christ's death was the death of our sins, Christ's resurrection is the quickening of our souls. Through him we have the remission of sin, and this is our quickening, for the pardon of the crime is the life of the criminal, which is owing to the resurrection of Christ as well as to his death. Whatever was in force against us is taken out of the way: the curse of the law is the handwriting against us, like the handwriting on the wall, cursed is every one who continues not in every thing, a handwriting which was against us and contrary to us, for it threatened our eternal ruin, and which was removed when he redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the death, the subject and the bond. Barnes says the readers were Gentiles giving unrestrained indulgence to the desires of the flesh, who lived as those who had not by any religious rite or covenant brought themselves under obligation to lead holy lives, and that the resurrection of the Lord Jesus was the means of imparting to us spiritual life. On the next verse he says the word rendered handwriting means something written by the hand, a manuscript, and here probably the writings of the Mosaic law; the allusion is probably to a written contract in which we bind ourselves to do a work or make a payment, and which remains in force until the bond is cancelled, which might be done either by blotting out the names, or by drawing lines through it, or, as appears to have been practised in the east, by driving a nail through it. The Jewish ceremonial law is represented as such a contract, binding those under it until it was nailed to the cross, so that the burdensome requirements of the Mosaic law are abolished and their necessity superseded by the death of Christ, which had the same effect as if they had been blotted from the statute-book, fulfilling them and introducing a more perfect system. That it was against us means against our peace, happiness and comfort: those ordinances bound and fettered the soul and restrained the expansive spirit of true piety which seeks the salvation of all alike, operating against the truly pious Jew whose religion would lead him to seek the salvation of the world, and against the Gentile, who was not in a situation to avail himself of them. They were necessary in order to introduce the gospel, but they were always burdensome, confined to one people, and if continued would operate to prevent the spread of the true religion around the world; hence the exulting language of the apostle, since the gospel contains nothing which is against or contrary to the true interest and happiness of any nation or any class of men. To take it out of the way is, in the Greek, out of the midst, that is, wholly removed; and the nailing means as if he had nailed it to his cross, so that it would be entirely removed out of our way. Ellicott notes that here, exactly as in Ephesians, there is a remarkable intermixture of the word we and the word you, the former conveying the universal statement of the gospel message of mercy and the other applying it emphatically to the Gentiles as Gentiles; through the Ephesian passage there runs a two-fold idea, the reconcilement of Jew and Gentile to God and the union of both in one Catholic Church, while in this Epistle it is only on the reconcilement to God in Christ that stress is laid. Here the deadness is spoken of as coming both from the actual power of transgressions and from the alienation from God marked by uncircumcision, whereas in the other passage the uncircumcision is looked upon only as a name of reproach. It is difficult, Ellicott says, to determine the subject of the sentence: according to all analogy it should be God, yet in the latter clauses it must surely be Christ; and since the fuller parallel passage shows an overt change of subject, a similar change is suggested here also, at the words and He hath taken it away. Speaking grammatically this introduces an anomaly, but such anomalies are not uncommon in Paul, especially in passages of high spiritual teaching. On the next verse Ellicott says the handwriting is the bond exacting payment or penalty in default, and that what this bond is we see from Ephesians 2:15, which speaks of the law of commandments in ordinances, there called the enmity slain by the cross. The metaphor here is different and especially notable as the first anticipation of those many metaphors of later theology in which the idea of a debt to God, paid for us by the blood of Christ as a satisfaction, is brought out. The Law is a bond, do this and thou shalt live, and on failure to do our part it stands against us; but God for Christ's sake forgives our transgressions and cancels the bond. It is a striking metaphor, full of graphic expressiveness, and is misleading only when we hold it to be not only the truth but the whole truth, forgetting that legal and forensic metaphors can but imperfectly represent inner spiritual realities. The change of tense at the taking away is significant: the act of atonement is over, its effect remains. At the nailing the idea of atonement comes in, since hitherto we have heard simply of free forgiveness and love of God, whereas now the bond is viewed as absolutely destroyed by Christ. It has been supposed, Ellicott notes, that there is allusion to some custom of cancelling documents by striking a nail through them, but the custom is doubtful and the supposition unnecessary; if any more definite allusion is to be sought, we might be inclined to refer to the title on the cross, probably nailed to it, which declared the explanation of the sufferer's death, the cancelled curse of the Law being just such an explanation of the great atoning death. Robertson calls the death moral death, and quotes the comment that they were dead in their trespasses and their alienation from God, of which the uncircumcision of the flesh was a symbol, the word being used merely in a metaphorical sense. The double compound verb rendered did he quicken together with is found only here and at Ephesians 2:5, apparently coined by Paul for this passage; probably God is the subject, because it is expressly so stated in Ephesians and because it is demanded by the phrase with him referring to Christ, and this can be true even if Christ be the subject of the verb hath taken away in the next verse. The act of forgiving is simultaneous with the quickening, though logically antecedent. On the next verse the participle rendered having blotted out is from an old verb meaning to rub out, wipe off, erase, and so cancelled; Plato used it of blotting out a writing, and manuscripts were often rubbed or scraped and written over again. The late compound rendered bond is very common in the papyri for a certificate of debt, the signature making a legal debt as Paul says to Philemon; many of the papyrus examples have been crossed out and so cancelled, and one decree is described as neither washed out nor written over. The handwriting in decrees was against the Jews, for they accepted it, but the Gentiles also gave moral assent to God's law written in their hearts, so Paul says against us and adds which was contrary to us, because we, neither Jew nor Gentile, could keep it; the double compound adjective so rendered occurs only here and at Hebrews 10:27. The perfect tense of the verb to take away emphasizes the permanence of the removal of the bond, which has been paid and cancelled and cannot be presented again. The verb rendered nailing means to fasten with nails to a thing; the victim was nailed to the cross as was Christ, and when Christ was crucified God nailed the Law to His cross, so that the bond is cancelled for us. Business men today sometimes file cancelled accounts, Robertson adds, but no evidence exists that Paul alluded to such a custom here.

Clarke and Wesley take the address and the bond. Clarke says the uncircumcision of the flesh must refer to that part of the Colossian Church which was made up of converted heathens, for the heathens alone were uncircumcised. On the next verse he says that by the handwriting of ordinances the apostle most evidently means the ceremonial law, which was against them, for they were bound to fulfil it, and contrary to them, as condemning them for their neglect and transgression of it, and which God himself has blotted out. Blotting out the handwriting is probably an allusion to the passage where the curses written in the book, in the case of the woman suspected of adultery, are directed to be blotted out with the bitter waters; and there can be little doubt of a further allusion to the custom of discharging the writing from parchment by the application of a fluid which dissolves the blackening principle of most inks. But the East India inks, being formed only of simple black and gum water, may be wiped clean off from the surface of the paper or parchment by the application of a wet sponge, so as to leave not one legible vestige remaining, which Clarke says he has often proved. When Christ was nailed to the cross, our obligation to fulfil these ordinances was done away; there may be another reference here to some ancient mode of annulling legal obligations by nailing them to a post, but Clarke does not recollect at present an instance or example, though antiquated laws are said to have been thus abrogated. Wesley says they were doubly dead to God, not only wallowing in trespasses, outward sins, but also in the uncircumcision of their flesh, which he calls a beautiful expression for original sin, the inbred corruption of the nature, the uncircumcised heart and affections. He supplies God the Father as the one who quickened them, making them partakers of the power of his resurrection, and adds that it is evident the apostle thus far speaks not of justification but of sanctification only. On the next verse Wesley says that where a debt is contracted it is usually testified by some handwriting, and when the debt is forgiven the handwriting is destroyed, either by blotting it out, by taking it away, or by tearing it, and that the apostle expresses God's destroying of it in all these three ways. This handwriting was not properly our sins themselves, which were the debt, but their guilt and cry before God.

debates: What the uncircumcision of the flesh means. Calvin allows a proper and a figurative sense and prefers the proper, uncircumcision being the badge and not the cause of alienation, on the ground that the context makes it no hindrance to sharing Christ's life; Wesley takes it figuratively for original sin and so makes the readers doubly dead; Robertson calls it merely metaphorical, a symbol of alienation; Clarke restricts the address to the converted heathens of the church.

Who quickens. Ellicott says analogy requires God while the later clauses require Christ, and places a change of subject at the words and he hath taken it away, granting the grammatical anomaly; Robertson keeps God throughout on the strength of the Ephesian parallel and of the phrase with him, while allowing Christ as the subject of the taking away; Wesley supplies God the Father without argument.

What the handwriting is. Gill catalogues four earlier answers, the covenant with Adam, the agreement at Sinai, God's book of remembrance and the book of conscience, and settles with Barnes, Clarke and Calvin on the ceremonial law; Calvin adds the reason, that every Mosaic ceremony was an acknowledgment of guilt; Ellicott and Wesley read it as a bond of debt.

Whether the nailing alludes to a known custom. Barnes reports an eastern practice of driving a nail through a contract to cancel it; Clarke suspects such a mode of annulling obligations but can recall no instance; Ellicott knows the suggestion and rejects it as doubtful and unnecessary, proposing instead the title on the cross; Robertson denies any allusion to the filing of cancelled accounts.
outliers: Ellicott alone warns against his own metaphor, calling the bond the first anticipation of the later theology of debt and satisfaction and holding that it misleads when taken for the whole truth rather than a part of it.
Clarke alone supports his reading from his own experiment, reporting that East India ink may be wiped clean off parchment with a wet sponge and that he has often proved it.

15.pericope_label: And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin identify the enemies and the chariot. Gill says the principalities are those of hell, the infernal powers of darkness, the devil that had the power of death, the accuser of the brethren, who often objected their debts, with all his works. Christ has divested these of their armour, wherein they trusted to have ruined men, as sin, the law and death; he has ransomed his people from him that was stronger than they and taken the prey out of the hands of the mighty; he has bruised the serpent's head, demolished his works, destroyed him and all his powers, and defeated all their counsels and designs against his elect. Gill notes that some render the word having put off, or unclothed, which some of the ancient writers apply to the flesh of Christ and understand of his putting off the flesh by death, whereby he gave the death blow to Satan and his powers, and that the Syriac version agrees, rendering it that by the putting off of his body he exposed to shame principalities and powers; but Gill thinks it may be better interpreted of unclothing or stripping principalities and powers of the armour with which they were clothed. Calvin says there is no doubt that the apostle means devils, whom Scripture represents as acting the part of accusing us before God, and that Paul says they are disarmed, so that they cannot bring forward anything against us, the attestation of our guilt being itself destroyed. He expressly adds this with the view of showing that the victory of Christ over Satan is disfigured by the false apostles, and that we are deprived of the fruit of it when they restore the ancient ceremonies; for if our liberty is the spoil which Christ has rescued from the devil, what do others, who would bring us back into bondage, but restore to Satan the spoils of which he had been stripped bare? The expression in the Greek allows the reading in himself, and the greater part of the manuscripts have it with an aspirate, but the connection of the passage imperatively requires that we read it otherwise, for what would be meagre as applied to Christ suits admirably as applied to the cross. As Paul had previously compared the cross to a signal trophy or show of triumph in which Christ led about his enemies, so he now compares it to a triumphal car in which he showed himself conspicuously to view; for although in the cross there is nothing but curse, it was nevertheless swallowed up by the power of God in such a way that the cross has put on, as it were, a new nature. There is no tribunal so magnificent, Calvin says, no throne so stately, no show of triumph so distinguished, no chariot so elevated, as is the gibbet on which Christ has subdued death and the devil, the prince of death, and has utterly trodden them under his feet.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the verb, the foes and the triumph. Barnes says to spoil is to plunder, as a victorious army does a conquered country, and that the terms used in this verse are all military, the idea being that Christ has completely subdued our enemies by his death, so that everything is now in subjection to him and we have nothing to fear. The principalities and powers are the formidable enemies that had held man in subjection and prevented his serving God, and there can be no doubt, Barnes thinks, that the apostle refers to the ranks of fallen, evil spirits which had usurped a dominion over the world: Satan and his legions had invaded the earth and drawn its inhabitants into captivity, and Christ by his death subdues the invaders and recaptures those whom they had subdued. To make a show of them openly is as a conqueror returning from a victory displays in a triumphal procession the kings and princes whom he has taken and the spoils of victory, which was commonly done when a triumph was decreed for a conqueror, prisoners being led along amidst the scenes of triumph. It was done openly, that is, in the face of the whole universe; but it does not refer to any public procession or display on the earth, but to the grand victory achieved in view of the universe. The words rendered in it may mean by the cross, or by himself, or, as Rosenmuller suggests, that God triumphed over these foes in Christ; the sense is substantially the same, that the triumph was effected by the atonement made for sin. The meaning of all this, Barnes says, is that since Christ has achieved such a victory and subdued all the foes of man, we should not be led captive but should regard ourselves as freemen, and should not be made again the slaves of custom, or habit, or ritual observances, or superstitious rites, or anything that has its origin in the kingdom of darkness. He notes that the argument of these verses is derived from what Christ has done for us, in four things: he has given us spiritual life, forgiven all our trespasses, blotted out the ordinances that were against us, and triumphed over all our foes. Ellicott calls this verse one of great difficulty, though not in the main idea, since the cross as usual is identified with the triumph over the powers of evil which it won, the very phrase made a show being cognate to the words put Him to open shame applied to the Crucifixion; the apparent triumph of the power of darkness over Him was His real and glorious triumph over them. Taking his metaphor from a Roman triumph, Paul represents Him as passing in triumphal majesty up the sacred way to the eternal gates, with all the powers of evil bound as captives behind His chariot before the eyes of men and angels; and it is to be noted that to this clause, so characteristic of the constant dwelling on the sole glory of Christ in this Epistle, there is nothing to correspond in the parallel passage of the Epistle to the Ephesians. The difficulty lies in the word translated having spoiled: that translation, as old as the Latin version, makes all simple and easy, but the original word certainly means having stripped Himself, as at Colossians 3:9, a word used by Paul alone in the New Testament and by him only in these two passages. Being forced to adopt that translation, Ellicott says the words admit of two renderings. First, having stripped from Himself the principalities and powers, that is, having stripped off that condition of the earthly life which gave them a grasp or occasion against Him; but this, though adopted by many old Greek commentators, seems singularly harsh in expression and far-fetched in idea, needing too much explanation to make it in any sense clear. Next, having unclothed Himself, He made a show of principalities and powers; and on the whole this rendering, although not free from difficulty on account of the apparent want of connection with the context, seems the easiest, since a strictly analogous word is used without an object following at 2 Corinthians 5:4, where the meaning is to put off the flesh. This is suggested still more naturally by the preceding phrase about the putting off of the body of the flesh, and accordingly many Latin fathers rendered it stripping Himself of the flesh, of which there is some trace as a reading or gloss in the Greek. Perhaps, Ellicott adds, Paul purposely omitted the object after the verb in order to show that it was by stripping Himself of all that He conquered: by becoming a show in absolute humiliation, He made the powers of evil a show in His triumph. Robertson says the verb occurs only here and at Colossians 3:9 and in one manuscript of Josephus, Paul simply combining two ordinary verbs for the expression of complete removal, and that two serious problems arise: whether God or Christ is referred to, and what is meant by the principalities and the powers. Modern scholars differ radically, and on the whole Robertson is inclined to look on God as still the subject and the powers as angels such as the Gnostics worshipped, and the verb to mean despoil rather than having put off from himself: in the Cross of Christ God showed his power openly without aid or help of angels. The verb rendered made a show is a late and rare verb from a word meaning an example, and so to make an example of; it is frequent in the papyri and occurs in the New Testament only here and at Matthew 1:19 of Joseph's conduct toward Mary, and no idea of disgrace is necessarily involved in it, the publicity being made plain by the word openly. The verb rendered triumphing is derived from a hymn sung in festal procession and is kin to the Latin word behind our triumph, a triumphal procession of victorious Roman generals; on the Cross the triumph was won, and God won a complete triumph over all the angelic agencies. It is possible, Robertson allows, to take the last words as referring to the bond, or even to Christ.

Clarke and Wesley take the custom and the agents, and part company over who is meant. Clarke says there is an allusion to the treatment of enemies when conquered: they are spoiled of their armour, so much the Greek verb implies, and they are exhibited with contumely and reproach to the populace, especially when the victor has the honour of a triumph, the first being answered by the words making a public exhibition of them and the second by the words triumphing over them. The principalities and powers, he says, refer to the emperors, kings and generals taken in battle and reserved to grace the victor's triumph; and it is very likely that by them the apostle means the rulers and chiefs in the Sanhedrin and the synagogues, who had great authority among the people both in making constitutions and in explaining traditions. The propagation of Christianity in Judea quite destroyed their spiritual power and domination, just as the propagation of Protestantism, which was Christianity revived, destroyed wherever it appeared the false doctrine and domination of the pope of Rome. The closing words, Clarke says, refer rather to Christ than to the cross, if indeed they be genuine, of which there is much reason to doubt, as the versions and fathers differ so greatly in quoting them; Griesbach has left them out of the text. Wesley says the principalities and powers are the evil angels, spoiled of their usurped dominion, that it is God the Father who exposed them openly, before all the hosts of hell and heaven, and that the triumph was in or by Christ; thus the paragraph, he notes, begins with Christ, goes on with him and ends with him.

Cyril turns the verse to the use of the sign of the cross. Let us not then be ashamed, he says, to confess the Crucified: be the Cross our seal, made with boldness by our fingers on our brow and on everything, over the bread we eat and the cups we drink, in our comings in and goings out, before our sleep, when we lie down and when we rise up, when we are in the way and when we are still. Great is that preservative; it is without price, for the sake of the poor, and without toil, for the sick, since its grace is from God. It is the Sign of the faithful and the dread of devils, for He triumphed over them in it, having made a shew of them openly; for when they see the Cross they are reminded of the Crucified, and they are afraid of Him who bruised the heads of the dragon. Despise not the Seal, Cyril adds, because of the freeness of the gift, but for this the rather honour thy Benefactor.

debates: What the verb means. Ellicott says the received rendering having spoiled makes everything easy but the word certainly means having stripped himself, and after weighing two constructions he prefers, having unclothed himself, he made a show of them; Robertson reports the same difficulty, says modern scholars differ radically, and settles for despoil with God as the subject; Gill knows the unclothed sense and the Syriac reading built on it, but prefers the stripping of the enemies' armour.

Who the principalities and powers are. Gill, Barnes, Calvin, Wesley and Robertson all make them evil spirits, Robertson specifying the angels the Gnostics worshipped and Calvin the devils who accuse us before God; Clarke alone makes them men, first the emperors and generals of a Roman triumph and then, as the apostle's likely meaning, the rulers and chiefs of the Sanhedrin and the synagogues.

Whether shame is part of the picture. Ellicott finds the phrase made a show cognate to the words put him to open shame, and Clarke says the conquered were exhibited with contumely and reproach to the populace; Robertson answers that no idea of disgrace is necessarily involved in the word, only publicity.

Whether the triumph was in the cross or in Christ. Calvin grants that the Greek allows in himself and that most manuscripts point it so, but holds the connection imperatively requires the cross, which he then makes a triumphal car; Clarke refers the words to Christ and doubts whether they are genuine at all, noting that Griesbach dropped them; Barnes allows either, and Robertson adds the bond as a third possibility; Wesley reads them of Christ.
outliers: Clarke alone reads the verse historically rather than of the unseen world, taking the principalities for the Jewish authorities whose power the spread of Christianity in Judea destroyed, and drawing a modern parallel from the effect of Protestantism on the papacy.

Ellicott alone turns the difficulty of the verb into the point of the verse, suggesting that Paul left the object out on purpose, so that by stripping himself of all and becoming a show in absolute humiliation Christ made the powers of evil a show in his triumph.
themes: made a shew of them openly
the cross as a triumphal car

16.pericope_label: Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin draw the conclusion and answer the objection about days. Gill says that since they were complete in Christ, had everything in him, were circumcised in him, and particularly since the handwriting of the law was blotted out and torn to pieces through the nails of the cross, the apostle's conclusion is that they should be judged by no man: they should not regard or submit to any man's judgment as to the observance of the ceremonial law. Christ is the prophet who was to be raised up like unto Moses, and who only, and not Moses, is to be heard; saints are to call no man master upon earth but him, are not to be the servants of men, nor should suffer any yoke of bondage to be imposed upon them; and should they be censured and condemned by others as if they were transgressors of the law for not observing the rituals of the former dispensation, they should not regard such censures, for the judaizing Christians were very censorious, ready to look upon and condemn a man as an immoral man and in a state of damnation if he did not keep the law of Moses. On the next verse Gill says these things were types, figures and representations of spiritual and evangelical things: the different meats and drinks, clean and unclean, allowed or forbidden by the law, were emblems of the two people, the Jews and the Gentiles, the one clean and the other unclean; but since these are become one in Christ the distinction of meats is ceased. The holy days or feasts of the Jews, the feasts of tabernacles, of the passover and of Pentecost, were types of Christ. Calvin says what the apostle had previously said of circumcision he now extends to the difference of meats and days, since circumcision was the first introduction to the observance of the law and other rites followed afterwards. To judge here means to hold one to be guilty of a crime, or to impose a scruple of conscience so that we are no longer free; it is not in the power of men to make us subject to the observance of rites which Christ has by his death abolished, and he exempts us from their yoke, that we may not allow ourselves to be fettered by the laws which they have imposed. Some understand the word rendered part to mean a portion, and Chrysostom accordingly thinks the apostle used the term because they did not observe all festival days, nor even keep holidays strictly in accordance with the appointment of the law; this, however, Calvin says, is but a poor interpretation and a very slender conjecture. He asks whether it may not be taken to mean a partition, for those that make a distinction of days separate one from another, such a mode of partition being suitable for the Jews, that they might celebrate strictly the days appointed by separating them from others, while among Christians such a division has ceased. Should any one object that we still keep up some observance of days, Calvin answers that we do not by any means observe days as though there were any sacredness in holidays, or as though it were not lawful to labour upon them, but that respect is paid to government and order, not to days. On the next verse Calvin says the reason the apostle frees Christians from the observance of them is that they belonged to a time when Christ was still in a manner absent, since he contrasts shadows with revelation and absence with manifestation; those who still adhere to the shadows act like one who should judge of a man's appearance from his shadow while he had the man himself personally before his eyes. The substance of what the ceremonies anciently prefigured is now presented before our eyes in Christ, who contains in himself everything that they marked out as future, so that the man who calls the ceremonies back into use either buries the manifestation of Christ or robs him of his excellence. To abstain from swine's flesh is in itself harmless, but the binding to do it is pernicious, because it makes void the grace of Christ. Should any one ask what view is then to be taken of our sacraments, whether they also do not represent Christ as absent, Calvin answers that they differ widely from the ancient ceremonies: as painters do not in the first draught bring out a likeness in vivid colours, but in the first instance draw rude and obscure lines with charcoal, so the representation of Christ under the law was unpolished and was as it were a first sketch, while in our sacraments it is seen drawn out to the life. They are not bare shadows but symbols, and while they represent Christ as absent to view and in distance of place, they testify that he has been once manifested and present him now to be enjoyed.

Henry concludes the chapter with exhortations to proper duty inferred from the foregoing discourse, and here cautions them to take heed of judaizing teachers, or those who would impose upon Christians the yoke of the ceremonial law. Much of the ceremonies of the law of Moses consisted in the distinction of meats and days, and it appears from Romans 14 that there were those who were for keeping up those distinctions; but here the apostle shows that since Christ has come and has cancelled the ceremonial law we ought not to keep it up. Let no man impose those things upon you, Henry says, for God has not imposed them; if God has made you free, be not you again entangled in that yoke of bondage. And this the rather because these things were shadows of things to come, which intimates that they had no intrinsic worth in them and that they are now done away. But the body is of Christ: the body of which they were shadows has come, and to continue the ceremonial observances, which were only types and shadows of Christ and the gospel, carries an intimation that Christ has not yet come and that the gospel state has not yet commenced. Observe, Henry adds, the advantages we have under the gospel above what they had under the law: they had the shadows, we have the substance.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson define the terms and weigh the sabbath. Barnes says the word judge is used in the sense of pronouncing a sentence: since they have been delivered by Christ from the evils that surrounded them and freed from the observances of the law, let no one sit in judgment on them or claim the right to decide for them in those matters, since they are not responsible to man for their conduct but to Christ, and no man has a right to impose that on them as a burden from which Christ has made them free. In meat means in respect to the various articles of food and drink, with undoubted reference to the distinctions the Jews made. The word rendered holyday means properly a feast or festival, and the allusion is to the festivals of the Jews, so that no one had a right to impose their observance on Christians or to condemn them if they did not keep them. On the new moon, Barnes explains that among the Hebrews, in addition to the daily sacrifices, two bullocks, a ram and seven sheep with a meat-offering were required to be presented to God, and that the new moon at the beginning of the month Tisri was the beginning of their civil year and was commanded to be observed as a festival. The word Sabbath in the Old Testament, he says, is applied not only to the seventh day but to all the days of holy rest observed by the Hebrews, and particularly to the beginning and close of their great festivals; there is doubtless reference to those days here, since the word is used in the plural and the apostle does not refer particularly to the Sabbath properly so called, and there is no evidence from this passage that he would teach that there was no obligation to observe any holy time. On the next verse Barnes says these were only a dim outline of future things and not the reality, and that between the things themselves which are in Christ and those which only represented or prefigured them there is as much difference as between a body and a shadow, a solid substance and a mere outline; having now the thing itself, the shadow can be to us of no value. Ellicott glosses the judging as imposing one's own laws upon another, and says the immediate reference is to the distinctions of meats under the Jewish law, now done away because the distinction of those within and without the covenant was also done away; but a study of Romans and of 1 Timothy 4:3, to say nothing of the tone of this passage or of the known characteristics of the later Gnosticism of the ascetic type, shows that these laws about eating and drinking were not mere matters of law but formed significant parts of a rigid mystic asceticism. The feast would seem to be one of the great festivals, the new moon the monthly and the sabbath the weekly solemnity, and Ellicott compares Isaiah and Ezekiel and Hosea, and the similar passage in Galatians, where the specially Judaic character is not so expressly marked. It is obvious, he says, that Paul gives no hint of any succession of the Lord's Day to be in any strict sense a Christian Sabbath; the Jewish Sabbath itself lingered in the Church as having a kind of sacredness, kept sometimes as a fast and sometimes as a festival, but its observance was not of obligation, and no man was to judge others in respect of it. On the next verse Ellicott says the spirit of the passage is precisely that of the argument which runs through the Epistle to the Hebrews, that the Law had a shadow of good things to come and not the very image of the things; when Paul deals with the legal and coercive aspect of the Law he calls it the schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, and when he turns to its ritual aspect he describes it as simply foreshadowing or typifying the substance, and therefore useful before the revelation of the substance, and useless or, if trusted in, worse than useless after it. Robertson notes the present imperative forbidding the habit of passing judgment in such matters, and says Paul has here in mind the ascetic regulations and practices of one wing of the Gnostics, possibly under Essenic or even Pharisaic influence, making a plea for freedom on a par with that of 1 Corinthians and Romans; the Essenes went far beyond the Mosaic regulations, and Josephus expressly explains the seventh day by the plural form used here. On the next verse Robertson notes that shadow is an old word opposed to substance: at Hebrews 10:1 it is distinguished from a picture, but here from the body, and the body casts the shadow and so belongs to Christ.

Clarke and Wesley limit the abolition and defend the sabbath. Clarke says the apostle speaks here in reference to some particulars of the handwriting of ordinances which had been taken away, namely the distinction of meats and drinks, what was clean and what unclean according to the law, and the necessity of observing certain holydays or festivals, such as the new moons and particular sabbaths, or those which should be observed with more than ordinary solemnity; all these had been taken out of the way and nailed to the cross and were no longer of moral obligation. There is no intimation here, Clarke insists, that the Sabbath was done away, or that its moral use was superseded by the introduction of Christianity: the command to remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, is of perpetual obligation and can never be superseded but by the final termination of time, since as a type of that rest which remains for the people of God it must continue in full force till that eternity arrives, for no type ever ceases till the antitype be come. Besides, he adds, it is not clear that the apostle refers at all to the Sabbath in this place, whether Jewish or Christian, his plural word most probably referring to their feasts of weeks. On the next verse Clarke says all these things were types and must continue in force till the Christ whom they represented came, so that the apostle says the body, the substance or design of them, was of Christ; the word shadow is often used to express anything imperfect or unsubstantial, while the term body was used in the opposite sense and expressed anything substantial, solid and firm, so that the law was but the shadow of good things to come and none should rest in it. Wesley says the meaning is to regard none who judge you, for not observing the ceremonial law in these or any other particulars, whether in respect of a yearly feast, the new moon, or the weekly Jewish sabbaths; and the shadow, he adds, is but a lifeless one, while the body, the substance, is of Christ.

Chrysostom traces the apostle's strategy and explains the words a part of a feast. Having first said darkly, take heed lest there shall be any one that maketh spoil of you after the tradition of men, and again, further back, this I say that no one may delude you with persuasiveness of speech, thus preoccupying their soul and working in it anxious thoughts, and having next inserted those benefits and increased the effect, he then brings in his reproof last and says, let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of a feast day, or a new moon, or a sabbath day. Seest thou how he depreciates them? If ye have obtained such things, he saith, why make yourselves accountable for these petty matters? And he makes light of them, saying, or in the part of a feast day, for in truth they did not retain the whole of the former rule. He said not, do not then observe them, but, let no man judge you: he showed that they were transgressing and undoing, but he brought his charge against others. He said not in clean and unclean, nor yet in feasts of Tabernacles and unleavened bread and Pentecost, but in part of a feast, for they ventured not to keep the whole, and if they did observe it, yet not so as to celebrate the feast; in part, he saith, showing that the greater part is done away, for even if they did keep sabbath, they did not do so with precision. Which are a shadow of the things to come: he means, of the New Covenant, but the body is Christ's. Some persons, Chrysostom notes, punctuate it, but the body is of Christ, that is, the truth is come in with Christ; others, the Body of Christ let no man adjudge away from you, that is, thwart you of it; and the term is employed when the victory is with one party and the prize with another, so that though a victor thou art thwarted. Thou standest above the devil and sin, he asks, why dost thou again subject thyself to sin?

debates: What the words a part of a feast mean. Chrysostom says the apostle wrote so because they did not keep the whole of the old rule and did not even keep sabbath with precision, the phrase showing the greater part done away; Calvin reports that reading, names Chrysostom for it, calls it a poor interpretation and a very slender conjecture, and proposes instead a partition, since those who distinguish days separate one from another; Barnes and Ellicott read it simply as the particular of a festival.

Whether the sabbath falls with the rest. Clarke denies it flatly, holding the command of perpetual obligation, since no type ceases till the antitype comes, and doubts the apostle refers to the sabbath at all; Ellicott says Paul gives no hint of a Christian Sabbath succeeding it, and that the Jewish sabbath lingered in the Church without being of obligation; Barnes takes the plural of the festival rests rather than the seventh day and denies that the verse proves no holy time binding; Calvin keeps days for government and order but not as holy.

Whether the ceremonies were merely legal. Ellicott holds that the rules about eating and drinking were not mere matters of law but parts of a rigid mystic asceticism; Robertson assigns them to one wing of the Gnostics and notes that the Essenes went far beyond the Mosaic regulations; Clarke and Henry treat them simply as the ceremonial law of Moses.
outliers: Calvin alone answers the objection his own argument invites, that the sacraments too represent an absent Christ, by making the ancient ceremonies a charcoal sketch and the sacraments the same likeness drawn out to the life.

Chrysostom alone reads the verse as a piece of tactics, observing that the apostle prepared the ground darkly, inserted the benefits, and only then brought in his reproof, and that he charged the judging rather than the observing.
themes: a shadow of things to come

18.pericope_label: Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, and not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the race and the Head. Gill says the allusion is to the Olympic games, one of which was running races, in which the race plot was fixed, a mark set up to look and run unto, and a corruptible crown proposed to be run for, held by one who sat as judge and determined who got the victory; these judges sometimes acted the unfair part and defrauded the victors of their proper right, and to such the apostle compares the false teachers. The Christian's prize is the incorruptible and never fading crown of glory, life and righteousness; the race plot is the Christian life, spent in the exercise of grace and the discharge of duty and in holding fast a profession of faith unto the end; and the mark he presses towards is Jesus Christ, so that his great concern should be lest by false teachers he should be defrauded of the prize of the high calling of God, through their removing the mark Christ from him. On the next verse Gill says that by making use of angels as mediators and intercessors, Christ the only Mediator, the Lord and head of angels and of the church, was dropped and laid aside, which is another reason the apostle gives why such men and their principles and practices should be shunned. Calvin says the apostle alludes to runners or wrestlers, to whom the prize was assigned on condition of their not giving way in the middle of the course, and admonishes them that the false apostles aimed at nothing else than to snatch away the palm, inasmuch as they draw them aside from the rectitude of their course, so that they must be shunned as the most injurious pests; the passage is carefully to be marked as intimating that all those who draw us aside from the simplicity of Christ cheat us out of the prize. Calvin reads the humility and the worship of angels conjointly, for the one follows the other, just as the Papists make use of the same pretext when philosophizing as to the worship of saints: having set forth man's unworthiness and preached of humility, they conclude that we must therefore seek for mediators to help us; but for this very reason has Christ humbled himself, that we might directly betake ourselves to him, however miserable sinners we may be. He notes that the worship of angels is by many interpreted otherwise, as meaning such as has been delivered to men by angels, since the Devil has always endeavoured to set off his impostures under this title, the Pope boasting that the trifles with which he has adulterated the pure worship of God are revelations, and the Theurgians of old alleging that the superstitions they contrived were delivered to them by angels. On the next verse Calvin says the apostle condemns in the use of one word whatever does not bear a relation to Christ, and confirms his statement on the ground that all things flow from him and depend upon him; hence, should any one call us anywhere else than to Christ, though in other respects he were big with heaven and earth, he is empty and full of wind, and we may without concern bid him farewell. He is speaking, Calvin observes, of those who did not openly reject or deny Christ but, not accurately understanding his office and power, sought out other helps and means of salvation and so were not firmly rooted in him. The Church does not stand otherwise than in the event of all things being furnished to her by Christ the Head, and her entire safety consists in him: the body has its nerves and joints, but all these derive their vigour solely from the Head. The constitution of the body will be in a right state if simply the Head, which furnishes the several members with everything they have, is allowed without hindrance to have the pre-eminence; and Paul speaks of the increase of God because it is not every increase that is approved by God, but only that which has a relation to the Head. We see, Calvin adds, that the kingdom of the Pope is not merely tall and large but swells out into a monstrous size, and since we do not there see what Paul requires in the Church, what shall we say but that it is a humpbacked body and a confused mass that will fall to pieces of itself.

Henry cautions them against those who would introduce the worship of angels as mediators between God and them, as the Gentile philosophers did. It looked like humility to apply to angels, as if men were conscious of their unworthiness to speak directly to God; but though it has a show of humility, it is a voluntary and not a commanded humility, and therefore is not acceptable, indeed not warrantable, since it takes that honour which is due to Christ only and gives it to a creature. There really was pride, Henry says, in this seeming humility: those who worship angels disclaim Christ, who is the only Mediator between God and man, and it is an insult to Christ, who is the Head of the church, to use any intercessors but him; when men let go their hold of Christ they catch at what will stand them in no stead. Besides, the notions upon which this practice was grounded were merely the inventions of men and not by divine revelation, the proud conceits of human reason which make a man presume to dive into things and determine them without sufficient knowledge and warrant, pretending to describe the order of angels and their respective ministries, which God has hidden from us. The body of Christ, he adds, is a growing body, and true wisdom is to keep close to the appointments of the gospel, in entire subjection to Christ, who is the only Head of his church.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the prize, the humility and the body. Barnes says the word used here occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and was employed with reference to the distribution of prizes at the Grecian games, meaning to give the prize against any one, to deprive of the palm, and hence to deprive of a due reward: they were to be on their guard lest the crown of victory to which they looked forward should be wrested from them by the arts of others, which would happen if they were persuaded to turn back or to falter in the race. Against an unjust judge, Barnes notes, we could have no power, but we may take care that the reward be not wrested from us by fraud. The word rendered humility means lowliness of mind, modesty, humbleness of deportment, and the apostle refers to the spirit assumed by those against whom he would guard the Colossians, the spirit of modesty or of humble inquirers: they would not announce their opinions with dogmatic certainty but would put on the appearance of great modesty, and in this way would become really more dangerous, for no false teachers are so dangerous as those who assume the aspect of great humility and manifest great reverence for divine things. The word rendered voluntary does not properly belong to the word rendered humility, but rather appertains to the later part of the sentence, and means that the persons referred to were willing, or had pleasure in attempting, to search into the hidden and abstruse things of religion. On the next verse Barnes says that not holding the Head means not holding the true doctrine respecting the Great Head of the church, and that this is essential to the maintenance of all the other doctrines of religion, since he who has just views of the Redeemer will not be in much danger of erring respecting other points of religious belief. Ellicott says the original is a word used almost technically for an unfair judgment in the stadium, robbing the victor of his prize, the prize here being the heavenly reward of the Christian course, and that there is a reference back to the sixteenth verse: there the apostle says, let no man arrogate judgment over you, and here, let no man use that arrogated judgment so as to cheat you of your prize, since there is one Judge who has right and who is righteous. The original of the next words is, willing in humility and worship, the phrase willing in being often used in the Greek Old Testament for delighting in, and the true sense is shown beyond doubt by the words used below, will-worship and humility. In this passage alone in the New Testament, Ellicott observes, humility is spoken of with something of the condemnation accorded to it in heathen morality, and the reason is obvious and instructive: humility is a grace of which the very essence is unconsciousness, and which, being itself negative, cannot live except by resting on some more positive quality such as faith or love; whenever it is consciously cultivated and delighted in it loses all its grace, becoming either unreal, the pride that apes humility, or turning to abject slavishness and meanness, of which depravations Church history is unhappily full. The worshipping of angels is closely connected with the voluntary humility, the link being the early growth of that unhappy idea, which has always lain at the root of saint-worship and angel-worship in the Church, that we must be brought near by angels and not by Christ, for that were too high a thing for us. With this passage it is obvious to connect the emphasis laid in Hebrews on the absolute superiority of our Lord to all angels and the prohibition of angel-worship in Revelation; and though it might seem strange that on the rigid monotheism of Judaism this incongruous creature-worship should have been engrafted, the worship of angels of which the Essenic system bore traces was excused on the ground that the Law had been given through the ministration of angels and that the tutelary guardianship of angels had been revealed in the later prophecy. On the next verse Ellicott says that in the failure to hold the Head lay the fatal error, since all these speculations and superstitions interfered with the direct hold of the soul on the mediation of Christ as the Head, from whom alone come all spiritual life and growth. The agreement with the Ephesian passage is nearly verbal, but the characteristic difference of idea is still traceable: there the body maketh increase unto the building up of itself in love, while here the increase is simply the increase of God, the increase which God gives and which grows into His likeness. In this passage there is also a greater scientific exactness, the joints and bands being the articulations and ligaments, whose two functions are the diffusion of nourishment and the knitting together of organic unity. Robertson says the verb is a late and rare compound meaning to act as umpire against one, perhaps because of bribery, occurring here only in the New Testament, the judge at the games being called by the simple form and the prize by another, so that it is parallel to but stronger than the verb used in the sixteenth verse. The participle rendered voluntary is a difficult idiom: some take it as like an adverb for wilfully, others make it a Hebraism from the Greek Old Testament usage, finding pleasure in humility, and one scholar suggested a compound meaning gratuitous humility. Humility is a virtue in the third chapter, but here it is linked with worship of the angels, which is idolatry, and so is probably false humility; they may have argued for angel worship on the plea that God is high and far removed, and so took angels as mediators, as some men do today with angels and saints in place of Christ. The verb rendered intruding has given much trouble, but it is an old word for going in to take possession, and inscriptions show it used of an initiate in the mysteries who set foot in and performed the rest of the rites, so that Paul is quoting the very word used of these initiates who take their stand on imagined revelations. The words vainly puffed up come from a late and vivid verb derived from a pair of bellows, a powerful picture of the self-conceit of these bombastic Gnostics. On the next verse Robertson notes that the negative used is the one of actual fact, so that this is a real case of deserting Christ as the Head: the Gnostics dethroned Christ from his primacy and placed him below a long line of aeons or angels, and did it with words of praise for Christ, as those do now who teach Christ as only the noblest of men. The headship of Christ, he says, is the keynote of this Epistle and the heart of Paul's Christology. The participles for being supplied and knit together are both present and continuous, and the words for joints and bands, the latter used by Aristotle and Galen of the human body, picture well the wonderful unity in the body by cells, muscles, arteries, veins, nerves, skin and glands, a marvellous machine working together under the direction of the head.

Clarke and Wesley read the humility as pretended and differ over the angels. Clarke says the first word means, let no man take from you the prize which the judge in the contests has assigned you, an allusion to the Olympic and Isthmian games: the Colossians had fought and conquered under the direction of Christ, who as the sole judge had assigned them the prize, while the false teachers, affecting great modesty, humility and sanctity, endeavoured to turn them aside from the Gospel. He then examines the terms: the word to will signifies also to delight; the word rendered humility signifies not only lowliness of mind but affliction of mind, and elsewhere to afflict the soul by fasting and self-abnegation; and the word rendered worshipping signifies reverence and modesty. Hence the passage has been paraphrased, let no man spoil you of the prize adjudged to you, who delights in mortifying his body and walking with the apparent modesty of an angel, affecting superior sanctity in order to gain disciples, intruding into things which he has not seen, and, notwithstanding his apparent humility, carnal in mind and puffed up with a sense of his superior knowledge and piety. It is very likely, Clarke says, that the apostle here alludes to the Essenes, who were remarkably strict and devout, spent a principal part of their time in the contemplation of the Divine Being, abstained from all sensual gratifications, and affected to live the life of angels upon earth; with their pretensions all that the apostle says perfectly agrees, and on this one supposition the whole passage is plain and easy. Many have understood the passage as referring to the adoration of angels, which seems to have been practised among the Jews, who appear to have considered them a sort of mediators between God and man, presenting the prayers of men before the throne; but this interpretation, Clarke judges, is not so likely as the foregoing. On the next verse he says that not holding the Head is not acknowledging Jesus Christ as the only Saviour of mankind and the only Head or chief of the Christian Church, on whom every member depends and from whom each derives both light and life. Wesley says that out of pretended humility they worshipped angels, as not daring to apply immediately to God, yet that this really sprang from their being puffed up, the constant forerunner of a fall, so far was it from being an instance of true humility. On the next verse he says that he does not hold Christ who does not trust in him alone, and that all the members are nourished by faith and knit together by love and mutual sympathy.

debates: Whether angels were worshipped at Colosse at all. Clarke takes the phrase of men who affected to live the life of angels upon earth and refers it to the Essenes, judging the reading that makes it adoration of angels less likely; Henry, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin and Gill all assume the adoration and dispute only its motive.

Why the humility is condemned. Ellicott says humility is a grace whose essence is unconsciousness, so that consciously cultivated it turns to the pride that apes humility or to abject meanness; Barnes says the modesty was assumed, and the more dangerous for being assumed; Henry calls it a voluntary and not a commanded humility, with real pride in it; Wesley says it sprang from being puffed up; Clarke alone treats the self-abasement as genuine asceticism rather than affectation.

What the worship of angels means. Calvin reports that many take it for worship delivered to men by angels, and notes that the Theurgians of old made that claim, though he reads humility and worship conjointly against the invocation of mediators; Ellicott and Robertson take it as adoration offered to angels as mediators; Henry takes it as honour due to Christ given to a creature.
outliers: Robertson alone finds the language of the mystery religions in the passage, showing from inscriptions that the verb rendered intruding was used of an initiate who set foot in and performed the rites, so that Paul turns the initiates' own word against them.

Calvin alone measures a church by the verse, holding that since only growth related to the Head is approved, a body that swells without it is humpbacked and a confused mass that will fall to pieces of itself.

20.pericope_label: Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances, (touch not; taste not; handle not;

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the union and the growth of such rules. Gill says the words do not signify any doubt but suppose the thing and press what is taken for granted: they were dead with Christ by virtue of union to him, being one with him and considered in him as their head and representative, so that they died in him and with him. They were crucified with him, as they are said to be buried with him and risen with him; they were dead with him by having communion with him in his death, and partook of the benefits of it, as redemption, pardon, justification and reconciliation; and they were planted together with him in the likeness of his death, so that as he died unto sin and lived unto God, so did they, and through the efficacy of his death were dead to sin, so that it was not imputed to them and could not damn and destroy them.
