On the next verse Gill says the apostle speaks not of himself but in the person of the Jewish doctors, who, urging the use of the ceremonial law to which they added decrees and constitutions of their own, said, touch not the dead body of any man, the bone of a man, or a grave, nor any man or woman in their uncleanness, not only their flesh but the bed they lay on or the seat they sat on, nor any creature that was by the law unclean, nor a Gentile or any notorious sinner; hence the Pharisees used to wash themselves when they returned from market, lest they should have been accidentally defiled by touching anything unclean, and there is a treatise in their Misna, called Oholot, which is full of decrees about things that defile by touching. They likewise said, taste not, neither the fat nor the blood of any creature which might be eaten, nor swine's flesh, nor the flesh of any creature that chewed the cud or divided the hoof, nor might the Nazarites taste wine or strong drink or vinegar. Calvin says the apostle had previously said that the ordinances were fastened to the cross of Christ, and now employs another figure of speech, that we are dead to them, as he teaches elsewhere that we are dead to the law and the law to us. The term death means abrogation, but is more expressive; the Colossians have nothing to do with ordinances, because they have died with Christ to ordinances, that is, after they died with Christ by regeneration they were through his kindness set free from ordinances, that they may not belong to them any more, and hence they are by no means bound by the ordinances which the false apostles endeavoured to impose upon them. On the next verse Calvin objects to the received rendering of the first word: since another word immediately follows which signifies the same thing, every one sees how cold and absurd such a repetition would be. The Greek verb, he says, is employed by the Greeks among its other significations in the sense of eating, and he cites examples from Homer and Xenophon, and from Plutarch's life of Caesar, where the soldiers in destitution of all things ate animals they had not been accustomed to use as food. This arrangement is both in other respects natural and most in accordance with the connection of the passage, for Paul points out imitatively to what length the waywardness of those who bind consciences by their laws is wont to proceed. From the very commencement they are unduly rigorous, and hence he sets out with their prohibition, not simply against eating but even against slightly partaking; after they have obtained what they wish they go beyond that command, so that they afterwards declare it unlawful to taste of what they do not wish should be eaten; at length they make it criminal even to touch. In short, Calvin says, when persons have once taken upon them to tyrannize over men's souls, there is no end of new laws being daily added to old ones, and new enactments starting up from time to time; how bright a mirror there is as to this in Popery. Paul therefore acts admirably well in admonishing us that human traditions are a labyrinth in which consciences are more and more entangled, nay more, are snares which from the beginning bind in such a way that in course of time they strangle in the end.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the premise, the speaker and the sects. Barnes says that in view of all that has been said, if it be true that they are really dead to the world, why do they act as if they still lived under the principles of the world? They died with Christ, such being the efficacy of his death and their union with him that they became dead also to the world; and the rudiments are the elements or principles which are of a worldly nature and which reign among worldly men. Why then do they allow these to influence them, as though they were living and acting under worldly principles? They ought no more to do so, Barnes says, than the things of this world influence those who are in their graves. On the next verse he says the three words seem intended as a specimen of the kind of ordinances the apostle refers to, or an imitation of the language of the Jewish teachers in regard to various kinds of food and drink, prohibiting men from even touching certain kinds of food, or tasting certain kinds of drink, or handling certain prohibited things. The rapid succession of the words, without any connecting particle, is supposed to denote the eagerness of the persons who imposed this injunction and their earnestness in warning others from contaminating themselves. Many injunctions of this kind are found in the writings of the Jewish Rabbins, and the ancient Jewish sect of the Essenes abounded in precepts of this kind: they allowed themselves no food that was pleasant to the taste, but ate dry, coarse bread and drank only water; many of them ate nothing until sunset, and if any one touched them who did not belong to their sect they washed themselves as if they had been most deeply defiled. Perhaps there was at Colosse a society of this kind, as there were in many other places out of Judea, and if there was, it is not improbable that many Christians imitated them. If this be the correct interpretation, Barnes says, then these are not the words of the apostle forbidding Christians to have anything to do with these ordinances, but are introduced as a specimen of the manner in which they who enjoined the observance of those ordinances pressed the subject on others. He adds that these words are often used as a kind of motto in reference to the use of intoxicating drinks, and express very well what is held by the friends of total abstinence; but it is obvious that they had no such reference as used by the apostle, nor should they be alleged as an authority or as an argument in the question about the propriety of the use of spirituous liquors. Intoxicating drinks should be abstained from, but the obligation should be made to rest on solid arguments and not on passages of Scripture like this; indeed this passage could with more plausibility be pressed into the service of the enemies of the total abstinence societies than into their support. Ellicott says the whole idea of the death with Christ and resurrection with Him is summed up by Paul in Romans 6, in direct connection with the entrance upon Christian life in baptism. The death with Christ is a death unto the life of the flesh, but this may be the life of sin, or it may be the outward and visible life of the world, and the latter is the sense to be taken here; such a life is under ordinances, under the rudiments of the world, or generally under law. In Galatians Paul brands as unspiritual the subjection to the weak and beggarly elements of mere ordinances. Of course, Ellicott adds, it is clear that in their place such ordinances have their value, both as means to an end and as symbols of an inner reality of self-devotion, and the true teaching as to these is found in our Lord's declaration to the Pharisees as to spiritual things and outward ordinances, that these things ought ye to have done and not to leave the others undone; in later times Paul declared with judicial calmness that the Law is good if a man use it lawfully. But to exalt these things to the first place was a fatal superstition, which both in its earlier and later phases he denounces unsparingly. On the next verse Ellicott says the first and last of the renderings should be inverted, since there is in the commands a climax of strictness: handle not the unclean thing, taste it not, touch it not with one of your fingers. It will be noted, he says, that all these commands are negative, not positive, and are marked by the ordinary ascetic preference of spiritual restraint to spiritual energy. Robertson takes the condition as one assumed to be true, and says the apostle is alluding to the picture of burial in baptism: having come out on the other side of the grave, we are not to act as though we had not done so. The verb rendered are ye subject to ordinances is a late and rare one made from the noun for a decree, and makes good sense either as middle or as passive; in either case they are to blame, since the bond of decrees was removed on the Cross of Christ, and Paul still has in mind the rules of the ascetic wing of the Gnostics. On the next verse Robertson calls the three prohibitions specimens of Gnostic rules, and notes that the Essenes took the Mosaic regulations and carried them much further while the Pharisees demanded ceremonially clean hands for all food; later ascetics, he adds, regard these prohibitions as Paul's own instead of those of the Gnostics condemned by him. Even today, Robertson remarks, men are finding that the noble prohibition law needs enlightened instruction to make it effective, which is true of all law; the Pharisees, Essenes and Gnostics made piety hinge on outward observances and rules instead of inward conviction and principle. The three verbs are all in the aorist subjunctive with the negative, a prohibition against handling or touching these forbidden things, and two of them do not differ greatly in meaning.

Clarke and Wesley gloss the terms and the objects. Clarke says they have renounced all hope of salvation from the observance of Jewish rites and ceremonies, which were only rudiments, first elements, or the alphabet out of which the whole science of Christianity was composed, and that the world and this world often signify the Jewish dispensation and the rites and services performed under it. Why then, as if they were still under the same dispensation from which they have been freed, are they subject to its ordinances, performing them as if expecting salvation from the performance? On the next verse Clarke says these are forms of expression very frequent among the Jews, and quotes a rabbinic passage: if they say to a Nazarite, don't drink, don't drink, and he notwithstanding drinks, he is guilty; if they say, don't shave, don't shave, and he shaves notwithstanding, he is guilty; if they say, don't put on these clothes, and he notwithstanding puts on heterogeneous garments, he is guilty. Wesley says the inference begun at the sixteenth verse is here continued and a new one follows at the beginning of the next chapter: if they are dead with Christ and so freed from the rudiments of the world, why do they receive ordinances which Christ has not enjoined and from which he has made them free? On the next verse he supplies the objects briefly: touch not an unclean thing, taste not any forbidden meat, handle not any consecrated vessel.

debates: Whose words the three prohibitions are. Barnes says they are not the apostle's own but a specimen of how those who enjoined such ordinances pressed the subject, and finds their eagerness in the rapid succession of the words; Gill says the apostle speaks in the person of the Jewish doctors; Robertson calls them specimens of Gnostic rules and reports that later ascetics took them for Paul's own; Wesley simply supplies an object for each.

Which way the three verbs move. Ellicott says the first and last renderings should be inverted, giving a climax of strictness from handling to tasting to touching with a finger; Calvin objects that the received rendering makes the first word repeat the third, shows that the Greek verb can mean to eat, and reads the order as the apostle mimicking how such rules grow, from forbidding partaking to forbidding tasting to making it criminal even to touch; Robertson notes only that two of the three differ little in meaning.

Whether ordinances have any value. Ellicott grants that in their place they serve both as means to an end and as symbols of self-devotion, citing our Lord's word that these ought ye to have done and not to leave the others undone, and locates the fatal superstition in exalting them to the first place; Calvin, Clarke and Wesley treat them simply as abrogated and no longer binding.

Where the rules came from. Gill traces them to the rabbis and names a treatise of the Misna on what defiles by touching; Clarke matches them with a rabbinic saying about a Nazarite; Barnes and Robertson both point to the Essenes, Barnes guessing that a society of the kind existed at Colosse and Robertson adding the Pharisees' demand for ceremonially clean hands.
outliers: Barnes alone refuses the verse to a cause he supports, granting that the words express the position of the friends of total abstinence very well but denying that the apostle meant anything of the kind, and remarking that the passage could be pressed with more plausibility against such societies than for them.

Calvin alone reads the three prohibitions as a history rather than a list, so that they trace the growth of tyranny over conscience from a first rigour to a final one, human traditions being a labyrinth that binds at the beginning and strangles at the end.
themes: touch not, taste not, handle not

22.pericope_label: Which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men? Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the perishing things and the three pretexts. Gill says the words may mean either the ordinances concerning touching, tasting and handling, which bring destruction and death on them that comply with them in order to obtain righteousness and life, so that instead of enjoying salvation through them they were the cause of damnation; or rather the meats not to be touched, tasted or handled, which are in their own nature perishing things and perish by being used. These are only of service to the body and can be of none to the soul; the using of them cannot defile the man, nor an abstinence from them sanctify him or commend him to God, since they relate only to this present life and can have no influence on the spiritual and eternal concerns of men. On the next verse Gill says the authors of these things set up for men of wisdom and were esteemed such, and their scholars who received their traditions and enforced them on others were styled the disciples of the wise men; they pretended that these constitutions of theirs were a hedge for the law, and for the honour of it, to preserve it and keep men from transgressing it, which carried in it some appearance of wisdom. Calvin says the apostle sets aside these enactments by a twofold argument: because they make religion consist in things outward and frail, which have no connection with the spiritual kingdom of God, and because they are from men and not from God. He combats the first as he does at Romans 14:17, that the kingdom of God is not in meat and drink, and as Christ himself says that whatever enters into the mouth defiles not the man; the sum is that the worship of God, true piety and the holiness of Christians do not consist in drink and food and clothing, which are transient and liable to corruption and perish by abuse, so that enactments are of no value in reference to things which tend to excite scruples of conscience. But in Popery, Calvin says, you would scarcely find any other holiness than what consists in little observances of corruptible things. The second argument, that they originated with men and have not God as their Author, is a thunderbolt by which he prostrates and swallows up all traditions of men, since those who bring consciences into bondage do injury to Christ and make void his death, and whatever is of human invention does not bind conscience. On the next verse Calvin says we have the anticipation of an objection, in which, while he concedes to his adversaries what they allege, he at the same time reckons it wholly worthless; for a show is placed in contrast with the reality, being an appearance which deceives by resemblance. Observe, he says, of what colours this consists: he makes mention of three, self-invented worship, humility, and neglect of the body. Superstition among the Greeks receives the name the apostle here uses, which literally denotes a voluntary service which men choose for themselves at their own option without authority from God; human traditions are agreeable to us on this account, that they are in accordance with our understanding, for any one will find in his own brain the first outlines of them. The second colour is humility, inasmuch as obedience both to God and men is pretended, so that men do not refuse even unreasonable burdens, and for the most part traditions of this kind are of such a nature as to appear admirable exercises of humility. They allure also by a pretext, inasmuch as they seem to be of the greatest avail for the mortification of the flesh, while there is no sparing of the body. Paul, however, bids farewell to those disguises, for what is in high esteem among men is often an abomination in the sight of God; such obedience is treacherous, and such humility perverse and sacrilegious, transferring to men the authority of God.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson divide the clause and construe the ending. Barnes says the clause about perishing is commonly marked as a part of the parenthesis or the quotation and that there is considerable difficulty in ascertaining its true meaning, but that it seems most probable these are the words of the apostle himself, thrown in in the rapidity of composition, and not to be connected with the phrase touch not. If so, the idea is that it cannot be of so much consequence as the Jewish teachers supposed to mark the difference between meats and drinks, since they were all to perish with the use of them and nothing was permanent about them; these ordinances had a value among the Hebrews when it was designed to keep them a distinct people, but had no value in themselves so as to make them binding on all mankind, and to suppose this was the common error of the Jews. According to this interpretation the twenty-first verse should be regarded as expressing the common maxim of the Jewish teachers and the clause before us as the words of the apostle, marked as a parenthesis. Many of the ordinances on which the Jews insisted were handed down by tradition and depended on human authority only, and of course should not bind the conscience. On the next verse Barnes says that the scrupulous observance of these precepts has a great appearance of piety and of regard for the will of God, and a show of wisdom too, or of a deep acquaintance with divine things, so that those who insist on them appear to be learned in what constitutes religion. Will worship is voluntary worship, that is, worship beyond what God strictly requires, supererogatory service; probably many of these things were urged not as strictly required but as conducing greatly to piety, the plea being that piety might be promoted by service rendered beyond what was absolutely enjoined, and that thus a spirit of uncommon piety would be evinced. There is much plausibility in this, Barnes says, and this has been the foundation of the appointment of the fasts and festivals of the church, of penances and self-inflicted tortures, of painful vigils and pilgrimages, of works of supererogation and of the merits of the saints; a large part of the corruptions of religion have arisen from this plausible but deceitful argument. God knew best what things were most conducive to piety for his people to observe, and we are most safe when we adhere most closely to what he has appointed. On the humility he says there is a great show of reverence for divine things in the manner in which they pursue their investigations and in their meek compliance with painful rites and ceremonies, in fastings, abstinence and penances; but under all this there lurks often the worst kind of pride, for pride may be pampered while the flesh grows lean. Neglecting of the body means putting on sackcloth and ashes, subjecting it to painful fastings and penances, and appearing in a form of squalid poverty, as if the body were not worth regarding; yet God made the body as well as the soul. Ellicott says it has been doubted whether the words about perishing are the continuation of the ascetic ordinance or the comment of the Apostle, but that the last word, which signifies not only using but using up, seems to decide for the latter: the things are things which go to destruction and are used up, and what permanent effect can they leave behind? He compares the saying that meat commendeth us not to God, and calls it an echo of our Lord's own teaching as to that which goeth into the mouth, and sees in the following words an allusion to Isaiah, quoted by our Lord in relation to these ceremonial observances. On the next verse Ellicott says it seems difficult to connect the words will worship and humility with the merely ceremonial observances immediately above, since they are almost an exact repetition of the description of the superstitious worship of the angels given earlier: will worship is nearly what we call superstition, the constant craving for objects to which we may find some excuse for paying reverence, and the prefix applies in sense to the humility also, a studied humility being either a pretence or a self-degradation; but in the words neglecting of the body, properly being unsparing of it in hardship, we pass to the ceremonial ordinances, and it is more than likely that the superstition and false asceticism were connected together, the latter being the condition of the supposed spiritual insight of the former. The last passage, Ellicott says, is difficult. Our version translates literally and would seem to regard the last words as simply an explanation, from the point of view of the false teachers, of neglecting of the body, and we certainly find that the Jewish ascetics did brand the most necessary satisfaction of appetite as a surfeiting of the flesh; but there is a fatal objection to this interpretation, that in that case Paul would leave the false pretension without a word of contradiction, which is almost incredible. Hence we must regard not in any honour as antithetical to the show of wisdom: the ordinances have a show of wisdom but are in no honour, that is, are of no value, and the common use of the word rendered honour for price or pay would readily lend itself to this sense. The only doubtful point is the interpretation of the last words, for the satisfying of the flesh, where there seems little doubt that the phrase is used in a bad sense, so that we must dismiss all reference to a right honouring of the body by innocent satisfaction of its needs. Some interpret it, of no value against the satisfaction of the flesh; but though the Greek will bear this sense, it is certainly not the common sense of the preposition used, and its adoption would expose the whole phrase to the charge of ambiguity. The other interpretation is, of no real value, tending to the satisfaction of the flesh; this is abrupt, but suits well the indignant and abrupt terseness of the passage, and gives, quite after Paul's manner, not only a denial of the neglecting of the body but a retort on the false teachers of the very charge they made against their opponents. Robertson renders the clause literally, are for perishing in the using, notes that the noun for decay is an old word while the noun for using up is late and rare, occurring in Plutarch and here only in the New Testament, and says these material things all perish in the use of them. On the next verse he says the phrase probably means the repute of wisdom, and that the word for will worship occurs nowhere else and was probably coined by Paul after the pattern of a word for voluntary slavery, to describe the voluntary worship of angels. Humility is here clearly in the bad sense, mock humility, and the next phrase is severity to the body, an old word meaning unsparing, found here alone in the New Testament, ascetics often practising flagellations and other hardnesses to the body. The closing words, Robertson says, are sharply debated along with the word for honour just before: it is not unusual for the preposition to be found in the sense of against rather than with or for, and the noun is an old word meaning satiety, occurring here only in the New Testament. One commentator is inclined to agree with others that there is a primitive corruption here, but the Revised Version rendering is possible; and it is true, Robertson adds, that mere rules do not carry us very far in human conduct, as every father or mother knows, though we must have some regulations in family and state and church, but they are not enough of themselves.

Clarke and Wesley define will worship and refuse it a value. Clarke says these things are not matters of eternal moment, since the different kinds of meats were made for the body and go with it into corruption, and in like manner all the rites and ceremonies of the Jewish religion now perish, having accomplished the end of their institution. The words about the commandments and doctrines of men, he says, should follow the twentieth verse, of which they form a part, and it appears from them that the apostle is speaking of the traditions of the elders and the load of cumbrous ceremonies which they added to the rites prescribed by Moses. On the next verse Clarke says all these prescriptions and rites have indeed the appearance of wisdom and are recommended by plausible reasons, but they form a worship which God has not commanded and enjoin macerations of the body accompanied with a humiliation of spirit that are neither profitable to the soul nor of any advantage to the body. What is here termed will worship signifies simply a mode of worship which a man chooses for himself, independently of the revelation which God has given; the whole system of Deism is such a worship, founded in the will or caprices of man and not in the wisdom or will of God. God will be served in his own way, Clarke says: it is right that he should prescribe to man the truths which he is to believe and the ordinances which he is to use, and to refuse to receive his teaching in order to prefer our own fancies is to light a farthing candle as a substitute for the noonday sun. From the beginning of the world God has prescribed the worship which was best pleasing to himself, and the nations which have either not had a revelation or refused the one given show by their diversity of worship, superstition, absurdity and often cruelty what the state of the whole would have been without it. Clarke adds that God has given directions concerning his worship and has appointed the seventh day for the peculiar exercises of spiritual duties, while other times he has left to man's convenience, and that they abuse the text who say that the appointment of particular times and places for religious service is will worship; God prescribes the thing and leaves it to man, except in the case of the Sabbath, to appoint the time and the place, nor is it possible to be too frequent in God's worship. Wesley glosses the perishing briefly, that these things have no farther use and no influence on the mind. On the next verse he says that not sparing the body means denying it many gratifications and putting it to many inconveniences, yet that these things are not of any real value before God, nor do they upon the whole mortify but satisfy the flesh, since they indulge our corrupt nature, our self-will, our pride and our desire of being distinguished from others.

debates: Whether the clause about perishing is quoted or the apostle's own. Barnes calls the point one of considerable difficulty but judges the words the apostle's, thrown in in the rapidity of composition, so that the previous verse is the Jewish maxim and this a parenthesis; Ellicott reaches the same verdict from the word itself, which means using up, so that the things can leave no permanent effect; Clarke differs on the arrangement, holding that the clause about the commandments of men belongs to the earlier verse.

What will worship covers. Clarke defines it as a mode of worship a man chooses for himself independently of revelation, and enters the caution that God prescribes the thing while leaving time and place to men, so that those abuse the text who call the appointing of times and places will worship; Barnes takes it as service beyond what God requires and traces to it the fasts, penances, vigils and works of supererogation; Calvin makes it a service chosen at men's own option, agreeable because anyone finds its first outlines in his own brain; Ellicott makes it nearly what we call superstition; Robertson says Paul coined the word.

How the last clause is to be construed. Ellicott rejects the literal rendering, since it would leave the false pretension uncontradicted, sets not in any honour against the show of wisdom, and prefers, of no real value, tending to the satisfaction of the flesh, as a retort of the teachers' own charge; Wesley states that reading plainly, that these things do not mortify but satisfy the flesh; Robertson allows that the preposition may mean against, reports a suspicion of primitive corruption, and leaves the Revised rendering standing.
outliers: Clarke alone defends the ordering of public worship against the verse, insisting that God prescribes the thing and leaves the time and the place to men, so that appointing particular times and places is not the will worship the apostle condemns.

Barnes alone turns the asceticism back on itself with a proverb, that under the sackcloth and the penances there lurks often the worst kind of pride, since pride may be pampered while the flesh grows lean.
